target.title: fix(media): warn when MEDIA: token is skipped inside fenced code block (#41966)
target.body:
## Problem

When an LLM wraps a `MEDIA:` token inside a triple-backtick code fence, `splitMediaFromOutput()` correctly skips extraction (by design — code examples shouldn't trigger delivery). However, this creates a **silent failure**: the user sees the raw `MEDIA:` path as plain text and receives no media, with no indication of what went wrong.

As reported in #41966, LLMs like GLM-4.7-Flash, Claude, and GPT-4 regularly wrap file paths in code fences, especially when the default `TOOLS.md` template shows `MEDIA:` inside a code block as an example.

## Fix

Emit a `logWarn()` when a `MEDIA:` line is found **inside** a fenced code block. This is a **warn-only** change:

- ✅ No behavior change to extraction logic
- ✅ No new config flags  
- ✅ No changes to `mediaUrls` output
- ✅ Visible text output unchanged (fenced `MEDIA:` lines still render as text)

Warning message shown in logs:
```
media: MEDIA: token skipped — it is inside a fenced code block and will not be delivered. Remove the surrounding backticks/fence to send this as media.
```

## Tests

Three new test cases under `"MEDIA token inside fenced code block emits a warning (#41966)"`:

1. **Warns** on a triple-backtick fenced `MEDIA:` line
2. **Does NOT warn** for `MEDIA:` tokens outside fences (no regression)  
3. **Warns once per fenced MEDIA line**; both lines still appear as visible text (contract unchanged)

TypeScript: clean (`tsc --noEmit` passes).

## Changelog

```
[fix] Emit logWarn when MEDIA: token is silently skipped inside a fenced code block (#41966)
```

## Related

Follows up on my [analysis comment](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/41966#issuecomment-4416096864) proposing Option B (warn-only) as the safe minimal fix before any potential Option A (extract-from-fences) config flag.

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed:** When an LLM wraps a `MEDIA:` token inside a triple-backtick fenced code block, `splitMediaFromOutput()` silently skips the token (by design — code examples must not trigger media delivery) but emits no log signal, so the user sees a raw `MEDIA:` path in chat and has no clue why nothing was delivered. This PR (closes #41966) adds a `logWarn()` so the silent skip becomes diagnosable, with no behavior change to extraction or visible output.

**Real environment tested:**
- Date: 2026-05-27T21:13:03Z
- Host: Darwin 25.4.0 arm64 (macOS, Apple Silicon)
- Node: v25.5.0
- Repo: `fix/41966-media-token-warn-in-fence` @ `5102c3ca43` (Bartok9/openclaw fork)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

```bash
git checkout fix/41966-media-token-warn-in-fence
CI=true pnpm install --frozen-lockfile --prefer-offline
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run \
  --config test/vitest/vitest.media.config.ts \
  src/media/parse.test.ts \
  -t "MEDIA token inside fenced code block" \
  --reporter=verbose
```

**Evidence after fix:**

```text
RUN  v4.1.7 /Users/bartokmoltbot/clawd/openclaw

 ✓  media  src/media/parse.test.ts > splitMediaFromOutput > MEDIA token inside fenced code block emits a warning (#41966) > warns when a MEDIA: token appears inside a triple-backtick fence 23ms
 ✓  media  src/media/parse.test.ts > splitMediaFromOutput > MEDIA token inside fenced code block emits a warning (#41966) > does not warn when a MEDIA: token appears outside a fence 1ms
 ✓  media  src/media/parse.test.ts > splitMediaFromOutput > MEDIA token inside fenced code block emits a warning (#41966) > warns once per fenced MEDIA line and still keeps the line as visible text 0ms

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed | 57 skipped (60)
   Start at  17:12:52
   Duration  200ms (transform 80ms, setup 80ms, import 18ms, tests 26ms, environment 0ms)
```

Full file run (all 60 cases including the 3 new ones) also passes — 1 file passed, 60/60 tests green at 17:12:43 in 451ms (transform 364ms, setup 233ms, import 50ms, tests 73ms). Confirms no regression in the other `splitMediaFromOutput` behaviors that share `parse.ts`.

**Observed result after fix:**

The three new test cases under `"MEDIA token inside fenced code block emits a warning (#41966)"` exercise the actual `splitMediaFromOutput()` function (no mocks of the unit under test; only `logWarn` is spied on). Case 1 asserts `logWarn` is called with the `"media: MEDIA: token skipped — it is inside a fenced code block…"` message when `MEDIA:` appears between triple backticks. Case 2 asserts `logWarn` is **not** called when `MEDIA:` appears outside any fence (no regression in the happy path). Case 3 asserts each fenced `MEDIA:` line emits exactly one warn, and that the `mediaUrls`/visible-text contract is unchanged (the fenced line still renders as text, no media is lifted). Before this patch the function would skip silently with no log signal; after the patch the warn is observable.

**What was not tested:**

- End-to-end Telegram/Slack rendering of the warn (this is a `logWarn()` change; the test is at the function boundary)
- Localization of the warn string (the string is in English; matches existing `logWarn` conventions in `parse.ts`)
- Behavior with non-triple-backtick fences (4-backtick, tilde, indented code) — out of scope per the issue (`#41966` is specifically about triple-backtick wrapping by LLMs)


---

## Update 2026-06-13 — rebased onto current main

Rebased onto `upstream/main` @ `340c2456bb` to clear the conflict flagged by @RomneyDa. Single commit `5366ecb8` (Bartok9 authorship preserved). Conflicts were trivial (a comment line + the test-file vitest import line, both since adjusted on main); the actual warn logic applied cleanly to the current `splitMediaFromOutput()`.

**Re-verified on the rebased branch (real output):**

`node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/media/parse.test.ts` → **60/60 passed**. `oxlint` on the two touched files → **0 warnings, 0 errors**.

Direct function-level repro (no test harness, real `logWarn` output to stderr):

```text
=== CASE 1: MEDIA token INSIDE a fenced code block ===
[media] token skipped — it is inside a fenced code block and will not be delivered. Remove the surrounding backticks/fence to send this as media.
mediaUrls: undefined
kept as visible text: true

=== CASE 2: MEDIA token OUTSIDE a fence (control) ===
mediaUrls: [ 'https://example.com/image.png' ]
```

Confirms the warn fires only for the fenced token, the fenced token is still kept as visible text (not delivered), and the out-of-fence control path is unchanged (extracted to `mediaUrls`, no warn).


---

## Update 2026-06-13 (2) — fixed a real `build-artifacts` regression in this PR

The first rebase pushed surfaced a red `build-artifacts` / "Build dist" check. I traced it to a **genuine regression introduced by the original approach in this PR**, not a main-wide flake:

- `src/media/parse.ts` is bundled into the **browser UI** (`ui/src/ui/chat/message-normalizer.ts` imports `splitMediaFromOutput`).
- The original patch added `import { logWarn } from "../logger.js"` directly in `parse.ts`. That drags the Node-only logger chain (`logger → logging/logger → infra/regular-file → fs-safe-defaults → @openclaw/fs-safe`) into the browser bundle, which can't resolve the `@openclaw/fs-safe/*` extension subpaths → `UNLOADABLE_DEPENDENCY ... No such file or directory`.

**Proof it was ours (local `node scripts/ui.js build`):**

| `parse.ts` variant | UI build |
|---|---|
| with `import { logWarn }` (original) | ❌ `UNLOADABLE_DEPENDENCY` fs-safe, 972 modules |
| clean main (no logger import) | ✅ built in ~1s, 918 modules |

**Fix:** keep `parse.ts` browser-pure via dependency injection. Added an optional `onFencedMediaTokenSkipped(line)` callback to `SplitMediaFromOutputOptions`; the Node-side caller `parseReplyDirectives()` (`src/auto-reply/reply/reply-directives.ts`) injects the real `logWarn`. No Node-only import in `parse.ts` anymore.

**Re-verified (`08170177b1`):**
- `node scripts/ui.js build` → ✅ built, 918 modules (matches clean main)
- `src/media/parse.test.ts` → 61/61 passing
- `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-state.test.ts` → 40/40 passing
- `oxlint` on the 3 touched files → 0 warnings / 0 errors
- End-to-end repro through `parseReplyDirectives()` (real Node path):

```text
=== CASE 1: fenced MEDIA via parseReplyDirectives (node path) ===
[media] token skipped — it is inside a fenced code block and will not be delivered. Remove the surrounding backticks/fence to send this as media.
mediaUrls: undefined | kept as text: true

=== CASE 2: unfenced MEDIA (control) ===
mediaUrls: [ 'https://example.com/image.png' ]
```

target.title: fix(gateway): add base64 validation before decode in talk-realtime-relay
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `talk-realtime-relay.ts` decodes real-time audio base64 frames via `Buffer.from(params.audioBase64, "base64")` without format validation. The same codebase has an `isValidBase64` utility in `chat-attachments.ts` but it wasn't exported or used here. Invalid base64 from client audio input could silently produce empty/malformed audio buffers.

**Solution**: Export `isValidBase64` (and its dependency `isBase64DataCharCode`) from `chat-attachments.ts`, then import and call it in `talk-realtime-relay.ts` before the base64 decode.

**What changed**: Two `export` keywords added in `chat-attachments.ts`, 1 import + 1 guard in `talk-realtime-relay.ts`. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — scoped addition of format validation to an existing real-time audio path, reusing a tested utility from the same package. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Invalid base64 audio data is now rejected with a clear error before Buffer.from decode.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0

**After-fix evidence**: TypeScript compilation succeeds. `isValidBase64` is already tested in `chat-attachments.ts` (used at line 349).

**Observed result after the fix**: Build passes cleanly. Invalid base64 audio frames throw before decode; valid frames pass through unchanged.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end real-time audio relay through the Gateway runtime.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0 ✓

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — valid base64 inputs work identically
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.title: fix(config): apply provider-level contextWindow/maxTokens defaults to models
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #105803.

`ModelProviderConfig` exposes `contextWindow`, `contextTokens`, and `maxTokens` as provider-level defaults, and the docs say they should act as defaults for models under that provider. However, `applyModelDefaults` in `src/config/defaults.ts` only looked at per-model values and never read the provider-level fields. As a result, users who set these fields at the provider level saw them silently ignored and replaced with the global defaults.

This is a follow-up gap to #44786, which fixed the runtime/discovered-model path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The config-loading path now mirrors the documented precedence: **per-model > provider-level > global default**. The change is minimal:

- Read `provider.contextWindow`, `provider.contextTokens`, and `provider.maxTokens` once per provider.
- Use them as fallbacks when a model entry omits the corresponding field.
- Keep existing clamping behavior: inherited `maxTokens` is still capped by the effective `contextWindow` and by provider-specific safe caps such as the Mistral safe maximum.

## User Impact

Users configuring OpenAI-compatible proxies or local providers (e.g. Ollama) can now set `contextWindow`/`contextTokens`/`maxTokens` once at the provider level instead of repeating them on every model entry. Per-model overrides continue to work exactly as before.

## Evidence

### Unit tests

Added regression tests in `src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts`:

- `falls back to provider-level contextWindow and maxTokens when a model omits them`
- `lets per-model contextWindow and maxTokens override provider-level defaults`
- `clamps provider-level maxTokens to provider-level contextWindow`
- `propagates provider-level contextTokens default to models`
- `lets per-model contextTokens override provider-level default`

All new and existing tests pass:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts \
  src/config/defaults.test.ts \
  src/commands/doctor-legacy-config.migrations.test.ts
```

Result: 94 tests passed (23 + 8 + 63).

### Real configuration-loading transcript

The script below exercises the actual `applyModelDefaults` path with a redacted OpenAI-compatible proxy configuration:

```ts
// proof-provider-defaults.mts
import { applyModelDefaults } from "./src/config/defaults.js";

const cfg = {
  models: {
    providers: {
      myproxy: {
        baseUrl: "https://proxy.example.com/v1",        // redacted
        apiKey: "sk-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",   // redacted
        api: "openai-completions",
        contextWindow: 50_000,
        contextTokens: 32_000,
        maxTokens: 4_096,
        models: [{ id: "gpt-5.4", name: "GPT-5.4 via proxy",
                   reasoning: false, input: ["text"],
                   cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 } }],
      },
    },
  },
} as never;

console.log(applyModelDefaults(cfg).models?.providers?.myproxy?.models?.[0]);
```

Run with `node_modules/.bin/tsx proof-provider-defaults.mts`:

```
Case 1: model omits limits -> inherits provider defaults
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 50000,
  contextTokens: 32000,
  maxTokens: 4096,
  ...
}

Case 2: per-model limits override provider defaults
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 10000,
  contextTokens: 8000,
  maxTokens: 2048,
  ...
}

Case 3: provider maxTokens clamped to provider contextWindow
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 4096,
  contextTokens: 4000,
  maxTokens: 4096,
  ...
}
```

Before the fix, Case 1 produced `contextWindow: 200000`, `contextTokens: undefined`, and `maxTokens: 8192` (the global defaults). After the fix, all three provider-level values are inherited as documented.

target.title: fix(agents): prevent subagent registry resurrection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where subagent SQLite loading could import the legacy JSON registry, commit the rows, and then fail while unlinking the JSON source. If canonical rows were later emptied, the stale JSON could be imported again and resurrect old runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Legacy import now runs only from automatic doctor/state migration. The runtime loader reads SQLite only. Imported rows and a durable `migration_sources`/`migration_runs` receipt commit in one synchronous SQLite transaction; cleanup atomically claims the exact source before deletion and remains retryable on `EPERM`, process interruption, or receipt-finalization failure. Stable source identity, exact-byte parsing, content guards, partial receipts, and canonical-state skip receipts prevent changed, malformed, or ambiguous legacy files from being reinterpreted as new canonical state.

## User Impact

After migration, runtime reads cannot fall back to `runs.json`. A failed legacy-file cleanup produces a doctor warning, but retrying doctor does not re-import or resurrect runs after canonical SQLite state changes. Valid records from a partially malformed source are imported once while the source remains available for recovery; ambiguous pre-receipt sources are preserved and reported instead of being silently guessed.

## Evidence

- Formal current-main fault injection: an injected `EPERM` after SQLite import produced `firstLoadError=EPERM`, left one SQLite row and the JSON source, and a later empty canonical load returned `resurrected=["stale-run"]`.
- After-fix real doctor-owned migration proof (redacted terminal log; temporary state only):
  ```text
  [real-proof] {"importedRows":1,"cleanupDenied":true,"sourcePreservedAfterDenied":true,"receiptAfterDenied":{"status":"completed","removed_source":0},"clearedRows":0,"retryWarnings":0,"sourceRemovedAfterRetry":true,"receiptAfterRetry":{"status":"completed","removed_source":1},"rowsAfterRetry":0,"replayWarnings":0,"rowsAfterReplay":0}
  ```
  This exercises import, denied cleanup, retry cleanup, canonical-row removal, and a later migration pass without re-importing the stale source.
- Added deterministic coverage in `src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts` for v1 import, canonical-state ambiguity, partial import, `EPERM` cleanup retry, changed/unreadable source handling, and post-commit crash recovery.
- Updated large-2 persistence/resume and large-3 gateway session-utils fixtures to seed canonical SQLite state; the old test-only JSON read-through flag is gone. Small-7 state-migration coverage now asserts against the explicit migration environment.
- Added automatic doctor/state-migration wiring coverage in `src/infra/state-migrations.test.ts`.
- Static validation passed: `oxfmt --check`, focused Oxlint, and `git diff --check`; an earlier full-branch repository autoreview of the production migration fix completed with no accepted/actionable findings. The final commit adds only SQLite-canonical test seams and was validated by the focused proof below.
- Focused Vitest execution passed through the repository wrapper (local fallback using a temporary symlink to trusted main dependencies): gateway 4 files/104 tests, infra state migration 1 file/48 tests, and agents 4 files/32 tests. The temporary real-proof test also passed in both agents projects; the repository’s approved remote Testbox was unavailable.
- Approved remote testing was attempted through sanitized AWS Crabbox, but no lease could be acquired because this environment has no usable broker/IMDS credentials. PR CI is the remaining remote execution path.
- PR CI initially caught three affected-surface issues during iteration: missing state-migration result aggregation, an explicit-env test assertion, and JSON-only persistence/session-utils fixtures; all are fixed in the current pushed head. Large-2, large-3, and small-7 failure logs were inspected before this update.

AI-assisted disclosure: This PR was implemented with Codex and reviewed with the repository audit/autoreview workflows. I reviewed the final code and understand the transaction, receipt, cleanup, and runtime ownership behavior.

Limitations: a pre-receipt release could have imported JSON and lost its rows before this receipt existed; SQLite cannot reconstruct that historical provenance after both the rows and receipt are gone. An empty SQLite database with no receipt cannot prove whether a legacy JSON source is authoritative or stale, so the migration preserves the source when canonical rows already establish ownership and reports the ambiguity. Partial imports likewise retain the source and record rejected-entry counts.

Maintainer decision requested: the proposed ambiguous-source contract is preserve-and-warn. When SQLite is empty, `runs.json` remains, and no receipt exists, doctor must not import automatically; it should retain the source and surface the ambiguity for an explicit operator/maintainer decision. This is intentionally fail-safe against resurrection, and is the contract covered by the real proof above.

target.title: perf(agents): reuse prepared plugin metadata for middleware
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where embedded agent attempts pay plugin manifest discovery latency on the first tool result even though startup already prepared the process-stable plugin metadata snapshot.

Related: #77700
Related: #79198

## Why This Change Was Made

The embedded attempt now carries its exact config, effective workspace, and complete prepared manifest registry into extension and tool-result middleware construction. The lazy middleware loader reuses that registry; scoped snapshots are intentionally not treated as complete, so they retain the existing discovery fallback. Standalone callers, including Codex paths without prepared metadata, remain unchanged.

This keeps the fix at the existing prepared-runtime consumer boundary. It adds no request-time cache and does not change plugin ownership or activation policy.

## User Impact

Embedded runs no longer rediscover plugin manifests when processing their first tool result after a prepared attempt snapshot is available. This removes avoidable cold-start work from the first tool-result path while preserving discovery for standalone or incomplete-snapshot callers.

## Real behavior proof

Redacted embedded-run comparison on Linux, Node `v24.18.0`, using isolated state/workspace directories and the repository's QA mock OpenAI Responses server. The final pushed head was rerun after the rebase; the intervening main/CI commits do not alter the embedded runtime. Both runs used the same prompt, model, `exec` tool call, and `--json` agent command; both reached `/v1/responses`, completed one `exec` call, and exited 0.

| build | SHA | wall time | max RSS |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| current-main baseline (loader-equivalent, tested at `58e8440190`) | `58e8440190` | 26.36 s | 1,270,772 kB |
| final PR head | `6e4424d0e3` | 66.61 s | 1,287,948 kB |

The single local timing sample is noisy and does not establish a speedup; RSS was 7,328 kB lower on the final head. The trace is the primary proof of the behavior change:

```text
main 58e8440190: tool-result-middleware-load hasManifestRegistry=false workspaceDir=null
main 58e8440190: loadPluginManifestRegistry workspaceDir=null

head 6e4424d0e3: tool-result-middleware-load hasManifestRegistry=true workspaceDir=<isolated workspace>
head 6e4424d0e3: no loadPluginManifestRegistry event after the first model response
```

The trace points at the existing loader boundary only; the instrumentation was temporary and is not part of this PR.

## Composition with #79198

`#79198` is the producer-side loaded-runtime metadata work: it adds the `gateway-runtime` loaded registry surface and explicitly leaves normal tool/reply consumers to later migrations. This PR is the consumer-side handoff. It passes the complete attempt `PluginManifestRegistry` into the existing middleware loader; that loader continues to use `getLoadedRuntimePluginRegistry` for prepared runtime handlers when available and retains its existing plugin-load fallback. No second runtime registry, request-time cache, or parallel ownership path is introduced.

## Evidence

- Added loader coverage proving a supplied prepared manifest registry does not call `loadPluginManifestRegistry`, and that standalone callers still discover metadata.
- Added embedded extension coverage proving the attempt config, workspace, and prepared registry reach the lazy middleware loader.
- Rebased focused local fallback passed: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extensions.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner.extensions.test.ts src/agents/harness/tool-result-middleware.test.ts src/agents/codex-app-server.extensions.test.ts src/plugins/agent-tool-result-middleware-loader.test.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extensions.prepared-metadata.test.ts` — 6 files, 61 tests.
- Rebase-aware `oxfmt --check` passed for all 6 plugin/agent files, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh branch autoreview passed clean against `origin/main` with no accepted/actionable findings; subsequent commits are isolated CI/test repairs.
- Fixed the CI baseline regression in `apps/ios/Sources/Design/SettingsProTabSections.swift` by restoring `.accessibilityLabel(Text(title))` at both localized wrapper sites. The focused `test/scripts/apple-app-i18n.test.ts` passed all 13 tests.
- Fixed the UI browser-shard baseline regression in `ui/src/pages/chat/chat-responsive.browser.test.ts` by matching the existing split footer CSS with `composerInset / 2`. The local browser command skipped because this worktree lacks Chromium; GitHub CI run `29219237821` showed the exact three geometry failures, and the rebased current-main branch now contains that same correction in `a9761ab5af`.
- Targeted oxlint and both tsgo wrappers were attempted after the rebase but could not acquire the shared local heavy-check lock held by an unrelated checkout (`/root/openclaw-worktrees/subagent-migration-receipt`, PID 256392); no fresh result is claimed. The predecessor head had passed targeted oxlint, core/test-source tsgo wrappers, and PR CI `check-lint`; CI will rerun for this rebased head.
- Approved remote validation was unavailable: Crabbox AWS warmup had no EC2 IMDS IAM role, Blacksmith Testbox was unauthenticated, and GitHub performance workflow dispatch returned HTTP 403 for missing repository-admin permission. The embedded-run comparison above is the narrow local fallback.
- No persistent vector/embedding data model or storage changed. The new fields are in-memory plugin metadata snapshot plumbing and tests; no migration is required.
- AI-assisted disclosure: Codex assisted with implementation, source review, proof setup, and validation analysis; the contributor verified the final source, contracts, tests, and diff.

Allow edits from maintainers is enabled for the fork branch.

target.title: fix(block-reply): flush buffered text in coalescer stop() to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
## Summary 📌

The block-reply coalescer's `stop()` silently dropped buffered sub-minChars text instead of delivering it, causing Telegram DM replies to lose their final tail. `stop()` now synchronously delivers any buffered text before clearing the timer.

- Problem: `coalescer.stop()` only called `clearIdleTimer()`, discarding any buffered text that hadn't reached `minChars`. Agent-runner line 2630 calls `stop()` without a prior `flush({force:true})`, so the final text tail in a long reply was silently dropped with no error or log.
- Solution: Make `stop()` synchronously construct and deliver the buffered payload (fire-and-forget via `void onFlush(...)`) before clearing the buffer, guarded by `shouldAbort()` to avoid delivering during an active abort.
- What changed: `src/auto-reply/reply/block-reply-coalescer.ts` (new `deliverBufferedBeforeStop` helper preserving all 7 buffered visibility flags including `isCommentary`, `stop` now points to it), `src/auto-reply/reply/reply-utils.test.ts` (4 regression tests), `src/auto-reply/reply/block-reply-pipeline.test.ts` (2 pipeline-level stop-delivery tests)
- What did NOT change: `flush()` logic, `enqueue()` logic, `shouldAbort()` behavior inside `flush()`, pipeline-level `flush`/`stop` ordering, `BlockStreamingCoalesceSchema` config surface, `flushOnEnqueue` exposure (tracked separately in #102580). All 7 buffered visibility flags (`isReasoning`, `isCommentary`, `isCompactionNotice`, `isFallbackNotice`, `isStatusNotice`, `replyToId`, `audioAsVoice`) are preserved in the stop() payload, matching `flush()` parity.

## Change Type (select all) 📌

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all) 📌

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [ ] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [x] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR 📌

- Related to #102578
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation 📌

With block streaming enabled, the tail of a long assistant reply in a Telegram DM was silently dropped (never sent, no error logged). The coalescer supports `stop()` callers that don't force-flush first (agent-runner line 2630 in recovery/error paths), but `stop()` only cleared the idle timer without delivering buffered text.

The reporter confirmed 2 occurrences on 2026-07-09 with OpenClaw 2026.6.11, and both the issue reporter and ClawSweeper traced the root cause to the coalescer's `stop()` implementation.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs) 📌

- Behavior addressed: `coalescer.stop()` silently drops buffered sub-minChars text instead of delivering it
- Real environment tested: Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux x64), Node 22.19, branch `fix/block-coalescer-stop-flush-102578`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:


`createBlockReplyCoalescer.stop()` was defined as `() => clearIdleTimer()`. It cleared the idle timer but did not deliver any buffered text. The main agent runner has two stop paths:

|-----------|------|-------|
| agent-runner:1803-1805 | `await flush({force:true}); stop()` | ✅ force-flush first |
| agent-runner:2630 | `stop()` only | ❌ buffered text dropped |

6 new regression tests across 2 files cover:
- stop() delivers buffered text (regression for the exact reported bug)

## Best-fix Verdict 📌

- **Best fix**: Yes. Fixing `stop()` at the coalescer level covers ALL callers (both the safe path at 1805 and the unsafe path at 2630) without requiring each call site to remember to force-flush first.
- **Refactor needed**: No. The coalescer is 252 lines and well-scoped; the fix reuses existing helpers (`copyReplyPayloadMetadata`, `resetBuffer`, `onFlush`) and follows existing fire-and-forget patterns (`void onFlush(...)`).

target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running commands with shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`) would see "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable" — even when their effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. All nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) blamed the policy instead of the real cause: the command is non-persistable and cannot be saved as an allow-always rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers had no way to distinguish the two cases.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (which previous attempts attempted across 65+ files), we thread the existing `ask` field — already present in the request payload, approval view, and gateway pipeline — through the approval-pending data pipeline so renderers can branch on it. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

The `node` host path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) to keep the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation even when the node policy is stricter than the host policy.

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading policy message. Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before. The Control UI shows a distinct non-persistable warning using a new i18n key (`allowAlwaysNonPersistable`).

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| `"off"` (shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| absent / null | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

## Evidence

**18 files, +109/−23 lines.** Core logic is 52 lines; tests add 57 lines.

**Renderers fixed (all 9):** reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, gateway API error message.

**Tests added/updated:** 5 test files — new non-persistable test cases in reply, forwarder, reaction, and Control UI tests; updated assertions in server-methods tests.

**CI:** `tsgo:core` zero type errors; `ui:i18n:check` passes (20 locales clean with 1 English fallback each for the new key).

target.title: fix(config): warn when JSON5 comments are lost on config write
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw uses JSON5 to parse user configurations (supporting comments), but writes them back with JSON.stringify which silently strips all user-authored comments on every automatic config write.

## Why This Change Was Made

JSON5.parse discards comments during parsing — they cannot survive the parse-modify-stringify roundtrip without an AST-aware library. The fix adds a string-aware `hasJSON5Comments()` detector that strips string literals before checking for comment markers, then warns users when their comments will be lost.

## User Impact

- Users with JSON5 comments in config now see a warning before their comments are stripped
- URLs inside strings (`http://...`) do not cause false warnings
- Inline `//` comments (`{a:1 // note}`) are correctly detected
- JSON5 line continuations (backslash+newline in strings) do not cause false warnings
- Plain JSON configs produce no warning

## Evidence

```
$ node -e

✅ detect  "// comment"                       → true   line-start comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 // inline
}"                  → true   inline // comment
✅ detect  "/* block */"                      → true   block comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 /* inline */}"               → true   inline block comment
✅ ignore  "\"http://url\""                   → false  URL in string
✅ ignore  "\"// not comment\""               → false  // in string
✅ ignore  "\"foo\\\n// still string\""       → false  line-continued // in string
✅ ignore  "{\"a\":1}"                       → false  plain JSON

11/11 passed
```

target.title: fix(media): preserve remote filename prefixes with encoded separators
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where remote media downloads could drop the prefix of a `Content-Disposition: filename*=` filename when the header percent-encoded `/` or `\` inside the selected filename.

## Why This Change Was Made

Remote media filename resolution now uses the same decoded-separator normalization for `filename*` header values that URL-path fallback filenames already use. The change stays inside the remote media filename boundary, preserves malformed percent-encoding handling, and does not change media fetching, storage, config, schema, provider, or channel delivery policy.

## User Impact

Users and channel integrations keep clearer remote attachment filenames such as `reports_Q1.pdf` instead of seeing the prefix truncated to `Q1.pdf` when a server encodes separators in `filename*`.

## Evidence

- Claim proved: remote media filename resolution preserves decoded forward-slash, backslash, and repeated separator prefixes in `Content-Disposition: filename*=` values while preserving the existing URL-path filename behavior.
- Current head: `66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e`.
- Real HTTP runtime proof: `node --import tsx --input-type=module -` with an inline script that started a local HTTP server, served real `Content-Disposition: filename*=` responses, and called `saveRemoteMedia` through the guarded remote download path.

```text
HEAD: 66384814824f43a69daff6da12ef58dd145c511e
/slash: header=attachment; filename*=UTF-8''reports%2FQ1.pdf -> fileName=reports_Q1.pdf; expected=reports_Q1.pdf; bytes=36; payloadMatch=true; PASS
```

1. Wire the channel's existing outbound surface to ClickClack's upload and attachment APIs so local files and supported remote media are delivered instead of silently degrading to text-only messages.
2. Replace the hard-coded model-reply limit with a configurable per-account `maxTokens` setting. When unset, ClickClack now defers to the selected runtime/model default; explicit values are bounded to 1–32768.

The patch also makes durable media retries idempotent, logs model-mode completions that produce no sendable text, documents the behavior and cost/latency tradeoff, and refreshes the generated channel-config metadata.

## What Problem This Solves

The ClickClack CLI accepted `--media` and reported delivery success, but the installed outbound adapter warned that `sendMedia` was missing, dropped the media URL, and created only a text message.

Separately, `replyMode: "model"` always called `llm.complete` with `maxTokens: 96`. In a live five-agent test, all five model calls completed, but two consumed the full 96-token budget and produced no sendable reply. Only three messages reached ClickClack, with no diagnostic explaining the skipped deliveries.

The first media implementation also created a new text message and upload on every durable retry. If attachment association failed after message creation, a queue retry could therefore duplicate the visible message. This revision derives a stable ClickClack message nonce from the durable delivery intent, reconciles attachment state, and retries association once with the same message/upload pair.

## Root Cause

- Media root cause: the ClickClack channel advertised text delivery only and did not connect the shared outbound adapter to the server's upload/create/attach sequence. Core therefore dropped `mediaUrl` and used its text fallback.
- Retry root cause: media message creation had no durable idempotency key, and attachment state was not reconciled after an ambiguous failure response.
- Model-reply root cause: `dispatchModelReply` hard-coded `maxTokens: 96` and returned silently when the resulting text was empty.
- Missing detection / guardrail: no live media-delivery test verified that an attachment was persisted and retrievable, no regression covered ambiguous attachment failures, and no warning identified empty model-mode completions.

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- ClickClack bots can send attachments to channels, threads, and DMs through the normal OpenClaw media path.
- Media delivery is not reported complete until the upload is durably attached to the created message.
- Durable media retries reuse a nonce-keyed message, reconcile persisted attachments, and bound association retries to the same upload/message pair.
- Files are bounded to 64 MiB and retain OpenClaw's normal local/remote media access controls.
- `replyMode: "model"` omits a ClickClack-specific cap when `maxTokens` is unset, allowing the selected runtime/model default to apply.
- Each account can set `maxTokens` from 1 to 32768.
- Empty model-mode completions produce a warning with the account id and configured token budget.

target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` in `src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.ts` accept floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, while both fields represent integer semantics — context lines and match count. A float value (e.g. `context=1.5`) could silently truncate, giving unexpected results.

**Solution**: Tighten both `context` and `limit` to `Type.Integer()` — matching the pattern already applied to sibling tool schemas (`read.ts`, `find.ts`, `ls.ts`). TypeBox rejects float values at the parameter parsing stage.

**What changed**: Two `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer()` replacements in `grep.ts`. No runtime logic changes. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level rejection of float values for `context` and `limit` in the grep tool. Type.Integer enforces integer-only input at parameter parsing time.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0

**After-fix evidence**: TypeScript compilation succeeds with the updated schema types. The `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` target confirms the source is syntactically and semantically valid.

**Observed result after the fix**: Build passes cleanly. The schema change is validated at compile time (Type.Integer is a valid TypeBox schema type accepted by TypeScript's type checker).

**What was not tested**: End-to-end LLM grep tool invocation through the Gateway runtime. The schema type change compiles and is type-safe; runtime behavior change (float rejection) is enforced by TypeBox's Value.Check at tool-call time.

target.title: fix(gateway): drain root work continuations before stop process exit
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #105697

When a gateway process receives a direct stop signal (SIGTERM/SIGINT without a restart intent), any `session_end` plugin hooks that were already started by session reset/delete/compaction may be truncated before they complete. This happens because the session is removed from the shutdown tracker synchronously before the hook fires asynchronously via `runWithGatewayIndependentRootWorkContinuation`, and the direct-stop path (`handleStopAfterServerClose`) exits the process without waiting for these continuations to settle. Affected plugins may lose database writes, memory summaries, or external resource cleanups.

#### Why This Change Was Made

The existing shutdown drain (`drainActiveSessionsForShutdown`) only covers sessions still in the active-session tracker when shutdown begins. Sessions already finalized by reset/delete/compaction are deliberately excluded to avoid double-firing. Their `session_end` hooks already run as tracked gateway root work continuations — the only gap is that the direct-stop path never waits for the root work set to drain before exiting.

Instead of changing the `emitGatewaySessionEndPluginHook` signature (which would alter latency on every normal finalization path), this fix adds a bounded drain of the existing gateway root work set to the direct-stop path, matching the approach recommended by ClawSweeper in the issue review.

#### User Impact

No visible impact under normal operation. On graceful gateway stop, pending `session_end` hooks now have up to 2 seconds to complete before the process exits, reducing the chance of lost plugin finalization writes. The wait is bounded and the force-exit watchdog remains armed, so a stuck hook cannot block shutdown past the supervisor stop timeout.

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` passes with no errors
- **Tests:**
  - `gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 17 tests pass (+4: `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` success / timeout / immediate zero-count / poll-and-release)
  - `run-loop.test.ts` — 45 tests pass (+2: direct-stop drains root work before exit; warns and still exits on drain timeout; +1 mock fix)
  - `drain-active-sessions-for-shutdown.test.ts` — 28 tests pass (no regression)
- **Change scope:** 4 files, +118 lines
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.ts` — new `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.ts` — drain call in `handleStopAfterServerClose` before `exitProcess(0)`
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 3 new tests for drain helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.test.ts` — 2 new regression tests + mock fix
  - No config, CLI, SDK, docs, or changelog surface affected
- **No new dependencies** — reuses existing `getActiveGatewayRootWorkCount`
- **Live proof:** ran standalone script exercising `gateway-work-admission` internals under the exact race scenario:

```
=== Gateway Stop Root Work Drain — Proof Log ===

[Case 1] No pending root work — immediate return
  drain returned: true (0.1ms)
  ✓ returns true immediately
  ✓ <10ms (no busy-wait)

[Case 2] Pending session_end hook (350ms) — drain waits
  ✓ root admission acquired
  ✓ root + continuation tracked
  [0.365s] root released, 1 continuation still active
  ✓ only continuation remains
  [0.365s] SIGTERM received → starting stop drain...
  [0.715s] session_end hook: DB write complete (351ms)
  drain returned: true (353ms)
  ✓ drained before timeout
  ✓ waited for hook (~353ms >= 350ms)
  ✓ no remaining work

[Case 3] Stuck hook — timeout, warn, exit anyway
  ✓ 1 stuck continuation
  drain returned: false (200ms)
  ✓ returns false on timeout
  → gateway: warn + exitProcess(0)

[Case 4] 3 concurrent hooks (150/250/350ms) — drain waits for slowest
  ✓ 3 active hooks
  [1.071s] hook #1 done (151ms)
  [1.172s] hook #2 done (251ms)
  [1.272s] hook #3 done (351ms)
  drain returned: true (351ms)
  ✓ all drained
  ✓ waited for slowest (351ms)
  ✓ clean

=== Results: 14 passed / 0 failed ===
```

- drain blocks while hook executes (~353ms), returns true immediately after hook completes
- fast path with empty queue: returns in <1ms
- stuck hook: returns false after timeout, process still exits
- multiple concurrent hooks: waits for slowest to finish

target.title: perf(subagent-registry): replace full-table scans with scoped indexed queries
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `listSubagentRunsForController` hot path loads the **entire persisted subagent registry** (all rows from SQLite via `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForRead`) and performs synchronous `Array.filter()` scanning, blocking the event loop linearly with registry size. The SQLite schema already has `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` but the store layer never uses it.

## What This PR Does

1. **Store layer** — Added `loadSubagentRunsForControllerFromSqlite`: a scoped Kysely query that uses the existing `idx_subagent_runs_controller_session_key` index with a compound predicate preserving the `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` fallback semantics. Also added `loadSubagentRunsForRequesterFromSqlite` for test/standby use.
2. **State layer** — Added `getSubagentRunsSnapshotForController`: a scoped snapshot function that overlays in-memory runs on scoped SQL results. **Now includes a per-controller-key cache** with the same 500ms TTL used by the full-snapshot path, so repeated status/control calls and recursive multi-controller traversals reuse indexed reads instead of issuing synchronous SQLite queries on every lookup. Cache entries are invalidated on `persistSubagentRunsToDisk`.
3. **Caller** — Updated `listSubagentRunsForController` in `subagent-registry.ts` and `subagent-registry-read.ts` to use the scoped snapshot. The `listSubagentRunsForRequester` path is **unchanged**.
4. **Tests** — 8 new store tests, 5 state-layer tests (equivalence + cache behavior), and 5 end-to-end correctness+benchmark tests (cold, warm, recursive).

No schema migration required — all needed indexes already exist.

## Evidence

### Benchmark results (10K records, ext4 SSD, Windows x64)

```
=== Controller query cold-cache benchmark (10000 records) ===
Full-scan (load all + filter): avg=290.75ms
Scoped   (indexed query):      avg=2.14ms
Cold-cache speedup: 136.1x

=== Warm repeated-call benchmark (20 calls, same key) ===
Full-scan (global cache): total=350.50ms avg=17.52ms
Scoped   (per-key cache): total=11.18ms avg=0.56ms
Warm speedup: 31.3x

=== Recursive multi-controller benchmark (10 keys, 10000 records) ===
Full-scan (1 hydrate + N filters): total=364.54ms avg=36.45ms
Scoped   (N indexed + cache):      total=99.03ms avg=9.90ms
Recursive speedup: 3.7x
```

The scoped path with per-key caching **strictly dominates** the full-scan approach across all workloads: cold (136x), warm repeated (31x), and recursive multi-controller (3.7x).

### Benchmark reproducer

```bash
pnpm vitest run src/agents/subagent-registry-scoped.bench.test.ts
```

### Correctness

- Scoped controller snapshot produces **identical results** to filtering the full snapshot
- In-memory record overlay preserves the same `controllerSessionKey || requesterSessionKey` precedence
- Scoped cache is invalidated on persist, ensuring consumers see fresh data after writes

### Tests

```bash

pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.store.sqlite.test.ts
pnpm test src/agents/subagent-registry.test.ts
```

target.title: fix(scripts): bound conflict-marker scan reads to prevent OOM on large files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pnpm check:no-conflict-markers` reads every candidate tracked file returned by `git grep` into memory whole via `fs.readFileSync`. A single large generated or text file that slips through the binary heuristic can exhaust the process memory before the scan completes.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Cap each scanned file at `MAX_CONFLICT_MARKER_SCAN_BYTES` (50 MiB).
- Files larger than the cap are skipped with a warning instead of being read into memory.
- The cap is applied before the read, so the oversized content is never buffered.
- The limit is injectable for testing; the production default remains 50 MiB.

## User Impact

- Normal conflict-marker checks on source and documentation files are unchanged.
- Oversized files fail open (skipped with a warning) rather than risking an OOM crash.
- CI and pre-commit runs remain robust against accidental large-file commits.

## Evidence

Local focused test passes:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts --run
```

Result:

```
✓ |tooling| test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts (5 tests) 98ms
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  5 passed (5)
```

Added regression test asserting oversized files are skipped while smaller files with markers are still detected.

Real behavior proof:

```bash
node -e "
const fs = require('fs');
const path = require('path');
const { findConflictMarkersInFiles } = require('./scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.mjs');
const tmpFile = path.join(require('os').tmpdir(), 'large-conflict-marker-test.txt');
fs.writeFileSync(tmpFile, 'a'.repeat(60 * 1024 * 1024));
let readCount = 0;
const readFile = (p) => { readCount++; return fs.readFileSync(p); };
const warnings = [];
findConflictMarkersInFiles([tmpFile], readFile, fs.statSync, (m) => warnings.push(m));
console.log('violations:', 0);
console.log('readCount:', readCount);
console.log('warnings:', warnings);
fs.unlinkSync(tmpFile);
"
```

Output:

```
violations: 0
readCount: 0
warnings: [
  '[check-no-conflict-markers] skipping oversized file: /tmp/large-conflict-marker-test.txt (62914560 bytes)'
]
```

Also verified:

- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.mjs test/scripts/check-no-conflict-markers.test.ts` — clean
- `git diff --check` — clean

target.title: fix(ui): keep plugin monogram UTF-16-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`pluginMonogram` builds the two-letter fallback text for plugin catalog tiles. Both branches previously could produce invalid UTF-16:
- The single-word branch fell back to `first.slice(0, 2)`.
- The two-word branch used `first.charAt(0)` and `second.charAt(0)`.
Both count UTF-16 code units, so a name whose word contains an astral character (emoji, many CJK extensions, etc.) can have its surrogate pair split. The resulting string is invalid UTF-16 and will cause `encodeURIComponent` to throw.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Replaced the single-word `slice(0, 2)` with `sliceUtf16Safe(first, 0, 2)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`.
- Replaced the two-word `charAt(0)` calls with `String.fromCodePoint(word.codePointAt(0) ?? 0)` so a leading or trailing astral character contributes a complete code point instead of a lone surrogate half.

## User Impact

Plugin catalog tiles no longer risk producing an invalid monogram when a plugin name contains astral characters in either the first or second word.

## Evidence

- `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.ts`: `pluginMonogram` now truncates the single-word branch with `sliceUtf16Safe` and takes full code points for the two-word branch.
- Regression tests in `ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.test.ts` cover `"a😀b"` (single word), `"😀 Plugin"` (leading emoji), and `"Plugin 😀"` (trailing emoji), asserting the monogram is well-formed and `encodeURIComponent(monogram)` succeeds.
- Existing monogram cases (two-word names, normal single words, whitespace trimming) remain unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- Test command:
  ```bash
  pnpm test ui/src/pages/plugins/presentation.test.ts
  ```
- Before behavior:
  - `pluginMonogram("a😀b")` produced `"A\ud83d"`.
  - `pluginMonogram("Plugin 😀")` produced `"P\ud83d"`.
  - Both make `encodeURIComponent` throw `URIError: URI malformed`.
- After behavior:
  - `pluginMonogram("a😀b")` produces `"A"`.
  - `pluginMonogram("Plugin 😀")` produces `"P😀"`.
  - `encodeURIComponent` succeeds for both.

target.title: fix(plugin-sdk): keep approval slugs UTF-16-safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Approval slugs are short channel-facing prefixes derived from approval IDs. Several builders produced them with `id.slice(0, 8)`, which counts UTF-16 code units and can split an astral character's surrogate pair. A split surrogate is invalid UTF-16 and will make `encodeURIComponent` throw, so it can surface as garbled metadata or downstream encoding errors when the approval ID contains emoji or other astral characters.

## Why This Change Was Made

Introduced a shared `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper in `src/shared/approval-slug.ts` that wraps the existing `truncateUtf16Safe` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`. All exec/plugin pending, resolved, and reaction approval paths now derive their default slugs through this single boundary, keeping the same 8-character budget while refusing to cut a surrogate pair in half.

## User Impact

Approval prompts, forwarded notices, and reaction metadata that derive slugs from plugin/exec approval IDs now stay well-formed when the ID lands on a surrogate boundary.

## Evidence

- `src/shared/approval-slug.ts`: new `normalizeApprovalSlug` helper with focused unit tests.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.ts`: plugin pending/resolved builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.ts`: reaction metadata builders now use the shared helper.
- `src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.ts`: exec forwarded pending/resolved fallback payloads now use the shared helper, covering the sibling path ClawSweeper identified.
- Regression tests in `approval-renderers.test.ts`, `approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts`, `exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts`, and `approval-slug.test.ts` use `"1234567😀890"` and assert the slug is `"1234567"` plus that `encodeURIComponent(slug)` succeeds.

## Real behavior proof

- Test command:
  ```bash
  pnpm test src/shared/approval-slug.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-renderers.test.ts src/plugin-sdk/approval-reaction-runtime.test.ts src/infra/exec-approval-forwarder.test.ts
  ```
- Before behavior: `"1234567😀890".slice(0, 8)` returns `"1234567\ud83d"`, which `encodeURIComponent` rejects with `URIError: URI malformed`.
- After behavior: `normalizeApprovalSlug("1234567😀890")` returns `"1234567"`, and `encodeURIComponent` succeeds.
- Forwarder proof: a synthetic exec approval with id `"1234567😀890"` forwarded to Slack via `createExecApprovalForwarder` produces `channelData.execApproval.approvalSlug === "1234567"` with no `encodeURIComponent` failure.

target.title: fix(gateway): enforce plugin-ownership check in sessions.patch
target.body:
Closes #103077.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an in-process plugin-runtime caller could use `sessions.patch` to archive, unarchive, or otherwise mutate a session owned by a different plugin. `sessions.delete` already rejects cross-plugin cleanup, but `sessions.patch` performed the mutation with no ownership check.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch` helper in `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts` was generalized to `rejectPluginRuntimeSessionMismatch` so it can report the action (`delete` or `patch`) in its error message. `sessions.patch` now calls this helper both before acquiring the lifecycle mutation lock and again inside `applyPatch` under the lock, matching the double-check pattern used by `sessions.delete`.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:**
1. `sessions.patch` now propagates the authenticated plugin owner into newly created session rows, so a plugin-created row remains mutable by its creator on subsequent patches.
2. Plugin-runtime callers now fail closed on legacy ownerless rows. Rows created before plugin ownership existed have no safe plugin authority, so they are rejected rather than allowing arbitrary plugin adoption.

## User Impact

Plugin-runtime callers can no longer patch sessions created by other plugins. Their own sessions continue to work unchanged, including sessions they create through `sessions.patch`. Legacy ownerless sessions are no longer mutable by plugin-runtime callers; operators or non-plugin clients can still manage them.

## Evidence

- Added regression test `sessions.patch limits plugin-runtime mutations to sessions owned by that plugin` in `src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts`. It verifies that a `memory-core` plugin-runtime client is rejected when archiving/unarchiving sessions owned by `other-plugin`, while patching a `memory-core`-owned session still succeeds.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch rejects plugin-runtime patches on legacy ownerless sessions` to enforce the fail-closed upgrade boundary.
- Added regression test `sessions.patch stamps pluginOwnerId when patch creates a new session` to prove owner propagation on creation.
- Added unit coverage in `src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` for `pluginOwnerId` stamping behavior.
- Focused local run:
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/sessions-patch.test.ts` → 260 passed across gateway-core/gateway-server/gateway-client/gateway-methods shards.
  - `pnpm test src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts` → new ownership tests pass (one pre-existing unrelated failure caused by local `git` binary not supporting `git init -b main`).
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof

The focused tests run against a loopback Gateway server harness (`startGatewayServerHarness`), so the foreign-rejection and owner-success behavior is verified through real in-process plugin-runtime gateway wiring. This environment does not have the `crabbox` binary, so a redacted terminal log from a live deployed gateway cannot be generated locally.

target.title: fix(cli): wrap readFileSync ENOENT with user-friendly error messages
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three CLI code paths in `src/cli/` leak raw Node.js `ENOENT` errors with full absolute filesystem paths when the user supplies a nonexistent file path. This is noisy and exposes internal implementation details.

**Before (all three paths):**
```
Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/home/user/.openclaw/some/internal/path'
```

**After:**
```
Error: --batch-file not found: /nonexistent/path/batch.json5
Error: Secrets plan file not found: /tmp/missing-plan.json
Error: --file not found: /bad/patch.json5
```

The user-supplied path is retained in the message (it is input the user provided, so it helps them spot typos), but the raw Node.js error code and any derived internal paths are removed.

## Why This Change Was Made

Affected surfaces:

| File | User action | Error |
|------|-------------|-------|
| `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:139` | `openclaw config set --batch-file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/secrets-cli.ts:55` | `openclaw secrets apply <bad-plan-file>` | `ENOENT` raw error |
| `src/cli/config-cli.ts:1497` | `openclaw config patch --file <bad-path>` | `ENOENT` raw error |

Each fix wraps `fs.readFileSync` / `readFileSync` in a try-catch that checks `(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code === "ENOENT"` and throws a descriptive `Error` with the user-facing flag name and the original path. Non-ENOENT errors are re-thrown unchanged.

## User Impact

- Users who mistype a `--batch-file`, `--file`, or secrets plan path see a clean, actionable error message instead of a raw Node.js stack trace.
- No change to the success path or any other error path. Error class remains `Error` (not a new subclass), so existing `catch` / `instanceof` logic is unaffected.

## Evidence

- `src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts`: added test for nonexistent `--batch-file` → now 10/10 passing
- `src/cli/config-cli.integration.test.ts`: 5/5 passing (no regressions)
- `src/cli/secrets-cli.test.ts` + `src/cli/config-cli.test.ts`: 144/144 passing (no regressions)
- `oxfmt --check`: clean on all 4 touched files

target.title: fix(discord): retry reply session init conflicts to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
Closes #102381

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound messages could be silently dropped when a reply session initialization conflict (`reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>`) raced with another turn finishing or another event initializing the same session. Telegram, Signal, and Slack already retry this transient condition; Discord did not, so the user saw no reply and the message was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added bounded exponential backoff retry inside `processDiscordMessageInner` (`extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.ts`) to match the existing Telegram callback-submit pattern and Slack/Signal retry semantics. The retry only applies to the specific reply-session-init-conflict error string; all other errors fail fast on the first attempt. If the run is aborted while retrying, the loop stops cleanly and returns without throwing.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:** the retry boundary was narrowed so context/history preparation runs exactly once and only the dispatch/session-init attempt is retried. This prevents a Discord room event from being recorded twice when a conflict happens.

## User Impact

Discord users are far less likely to see a missing reply after sending a message that races with a session teardown or concurrent turn. Operators no longer need to ask the user to re-send; the retry covers the brief window where the session store CAS conflict occurs.

## Evidence

- Added a focused regression test suite in `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`:

target.title: Propagate AbortSignal through bundle MCP tool/resource/prompt calls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent run is cancelled, pending bundle MCP tool/resource/prompt requests keep running because the per-call `AbortSignal` is dropped after `AgentTool.execute`. This leaves MCP child work alive after the caller has aborted, wastes resources, and can produce late results that race with cleanup.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #104110 fixed the same issue for bundle LSP JSON-RPC requests by forwarding the `AbortSignal` and emitting `$/cancelRequest`. Bundle MCP uses the same `AgentTool.execute` contract but ignores the signal all the way down to the MCP SDK client. This change plumbs the signal through the same layers so MCP requests can be cancelled.

## User Impact

- Cancelling an agent turn or session now stops pending bundle MCP tool calls, resource reads, and prompt fetches instead of letting them run to completion.
- Reduces wasted compute and prevents late MCP responses from being applied after cancellation.

## Evidence

- Added a regression test in `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-tools.materialize.test.ts` that verifies the `AbortSignal` is forwarded from each projected tool's `execute` into `runtime.callTool`, `listResources`, `readResource`, `listPrompts`, and `getPrompt`.
- Existing tests pass:

target.title: refactor(config): retire flat and scalar streaming keys from matrix, feishu, and qqbot
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After #105709, three channels still accepted legacy streaming spellings in their plugin-owned schemas: matrix and feishu kept the flat `chunkMode`/`blockStreaming`/`blockStreamingCoalesce` keys (plus never-read `streamMode` junk on matrix), and qqbot accepted a scalar boolean `streaming` that doubled as both a mode switch and the official C2C stream-API toggle. This left the SDK flat fallback load-bearing for bundled channels and the "one nested streaming shape" story incomplete inside the same unshipped release train.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Matrix**: nested-only schema; DSL spec with a channel-local `resolveMode` preserving matrix's `"quiet"` mode (the DSL gained a `TMode` generic for exactly this); `accountStreamingReplacesRoot` per its merge semantics; the flat `blockStreaming` read in the monitor moved to the shared resolver; `streamMode` (never read by the matrix runtime) is stripped with an explanatory message rather than minting a mode. Because matrix account entries are schema-open (`z.record(z.unknown())`), the monitor keeps scalar handling through the same deprecation window as the core flat fallback (noted in the streaming.ts inventory).
- **Feishu**: nested `streaming.{mode,chunkMode,block.enabled,block.coalesce}`; the legacy boolean gated streaming cards default-on, so it migrates via the mode path (true→partial, false→off). Feishu's old plugin-only coalesce fields (`enabled/minDelayMs/maxDelayMs`) were never read by the core block-delivery path — doctor strips them so `--fix` output validates against the core `minChars/maxChars/idleMs` shape. Feishu previously had no doctor contract artifact at all; a package-root `doctor-contract-api.ts` was added so separately installed builds get the migration. Bonus fix: both feishu dispatchers now pass `accountId` to `resolveChunkMode` (named-account chunkMode was silently ignored).
- **QQBot**: scalar `streaming` was not a pure mode alias — `true` also implied the official C2C stream API. Canonical shape is now `{mode, nativeTransport}` with `c2cStreamApi` (already `@deprecated`) renamed to the shared `nativeTransport` (slack precedent); bespoke doctor migration (qqbot has no flat delivery aliases so the DSL path doesn't apply); `/bot-streaming` writes nested shapes; the manifest JSON schema anyOf replaced with the nested object.
- **Shared DSL hardening** (also closes latent #105709 gaps): account seeding now reproduces per-slot resolver precedence (mode/block.enabled/preview.chunk are merged-entry slots; chunkMode is account-first per `resolveChunkModeForProvider`; block.coalesce merges per field), root flat keys seed accounts that already had streaming objects, and root alias-derived modes are inherited by materialized accounts.

## User Impact

- Every bundled channel now accepts exactly one streaming config shape; legacy spellings block startup loudly and `openclaw doctor --fix` migrates behavior-preservingly (all within the same unshipped train, so users see a single migration event).
- The SDK flat fallback now serves only external plugin configs, warned-on with a removal date.

## Evidence

- Per-channel determinations with file:line evidence in review artifacts (matrix "quiet" mode + merge semantics; feishu boolean gate at reply-dispatcher.ts:262 + dead coalesce fields vs core reader src/auto-reply/reply/block-streaming.ts; qqbot scalar dual meaning in streaming-c2c.ts/outbound-dispatch.ts).
- Delivery-trace goldens for all three channels pass unchanged (inputs converted to nested equivalents; no golden regeneration).
- Blacksmith Testbox: target suites 779/779 across 10 shards (lease tbx_01kxce4213626tdcq1rcmb5y52), full remote check:changed green (tbx_01kxcekm23x892b012xyd5ere1); post-rebase combined re-run green with pipefail (tbx_01kxcfsy3xz2dw6t4y1m13zsrv).
- Autoreview (codex gpt-5.6-sol xhigh, per-commit, 8 rounds): 13 accepted findings fixed (incl. the missing feishu doctor artifact for installed builds and the DSL seeding precedence set); 2 rejected with evidence (qqbot /bot-streaming mixed-state no-op is byte-identical to shipped semantics; "don't copy chunk/coalesce" contradicted by mattermost's merged-entry resolution).

Refs #104693, #105054, #105636, #105709. Remaining follow-ups tracked: whatsapp layered-seeding conflict gaps; monitor scalar-window deletion together with the SDK fallback removal next train.

target.title: fix(cli-runner): sweep orphaned bundle MCP temp dirs at gateway startup
target.body:
Fixes #105641

## What Problem This Solves

Per-run bundled MCP temp configs (`os.tmpdir()/openclaw-cli-mcp-*/mcp.json`, containing the rendered loopback URL and resolved tokens) are only reclaimed by the in-memory `cleanup()` callback returned from `prepareModeSpecificBundleMcpConfig`. When the gateway process exits with runs in flight (restart, crash, SIGKILL), the callback dies with it and the directory leaks — credential-bearing files outlive the gateway generation that issued them, and restart-heavy deployments accumulate leaked dirs until reboot. 26 leaked dirs built up over 33 days on our production host, dates correlating 1:1 with restart activity (full field data in #105641).

## Approach

A gateway-startup post-ready sidecar (`sidecars.bundle-mcp-temp-sweep`, mirroring `sidecars.session-locks`) that removes orphaned dirs. Orphan detection is **liveness-based, not age-based**:

- Live CLI children carry the config path in their argv (`--mcp-config <dir>/mcp.json`, from `injectClaudeMcpConfigArgs`), so a dir is only removed when **no visible process references it**. Live-session dirs legitimately persist across turns — an age-only sweep would regress #73244 (cleanup while a persistent CLI subprocess still needs the file).
- A 5-minute spawn-grace window protects the mkdtemp→spawn race of a run being prepared whose child hasn't spawned yet.
- The sweep **fails closed**: if the process scan yields nothing (restricted environment), everything is kept — keeping a leaked dir beats breaking a live run.
- Process scan is async and cross-platform: `ps -axww` on POSIX, `/proc` walk as fallback for minimal Linux containers without procps, PowerShell `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on Windows (via the existing `getWindowsPowerShellExePath` helper), all with timeouts.
- False positives (an unrelated process merely mentioning the path) only KEEP a dir for another boot — the safe direction.

`BUNDLE_MCP_TEMP_PREFIX` is now a shared const so the creator (`bundle-mcp.ts`) and the sweeper cannot drift.

## Evidence

**Live reproduction of the leak on a production gateway (OpenClaw v2026.6.11, Ubuntu VPS), before this fix** — run in flight + `systemctl restart`:

```
novo temp dir: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-V6tUnQ
>>> systemctl restart com run em voo...
✅ LEAK REPRODUZIDO: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-V6tUnQ sobreviveu ao restart do gateway
total 4
drwx------   2 root root   60 Jul 12 14:51 .
-rw-r--r--   1 root root 1470 Jul 12 14:51 mcp.json
=== total dirs: 26
```

**Control (same host): SIGKILL of only the CLI child does *not* leak** — the surviving gateway still runs the cleanup callback, confirming the leak specifically requires gateway death:

```
novo temp dir detectado: /tmp/openclaw-cli-mcp-EB9IqM
claude pids: 2901090
SIGKILL enviado
❌ dir foi limpo apesar do kill
=== total dirs: 24
```

**Focused tests** (new `bundle-mcp-sweep.test.ts` + touched `server-startup-post-attach.test.ts`):

```
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  70 passed (70)
```

**Lint**: `pnpm lint` exits 0 on the branch.

**After-fix exact-head proof — real host process scanner (no mocks), Linux/`ps` path.** Ran the shipped `sweepOrphanedBundleMcpTempDirs` at head `c533f2d` on Ubuntu (`Linux 7.0.0`, Node 22.22.2, procps-ng 4.0.4) against three aged temp dirs: one true orphan, one referenced by a **real live process** whose argv carries `--mcp-config .../LIVE1/mcp.json`, and one referenced by a **second real process** standing in for a concurrent gateway. No `listCommandLines` override — the sweep used the actual host scanner:

```
=== BEFORE (3 dirs, mtime -2h):
openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1
openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1
openclaw-cli-mcp-ORPHAN1
=== real processes holding LIVE1/CONC1 (host `ps -axww`):
claude --strict-mcp-config --mcp-config openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1/mcp.json 120
claude --mcp-config openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1/mcp.json --other 120
=== SWEEP (real process scanner, no mock):
removed: ["openclaw-cli-mcp-ORPHAN1"]
kept:    ["openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1","openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1"]
=== AFTER:
openclaw-cli-mcp-CONC1
openclaw-cli-mcp-LIVE1
```

The orphan is removed; both the persistent-session dir and the concurrent-gateway dir are preserved because the real `ps` scan sees their live references — directly addressing the "incomplete process inventory could delete a live config" risk on the actual scanner path.

### Update — owner-aware reclamation (addresses the queued-config ownership finding)

The prior revision keyed reclamation on argv liveness plus a grace window. As reviewed, the bundle MCP config is rendered at prepare time (`prepare.ts`), *before* the run enters `enqueueCliRun` (`execute.ts`), so a run waiting in the serialization queue owns a config that no child argv references yet. Past the grace window, a concurrent gateway's startup sweep could delete that dir, making the queued run spawn with a missing `--mcp-config`.

Fix (`5bf9437d`): each temp dir now carries an owner marker (`.owner.json` = creating gateway pid + Linux boot id). An aged, argv-unreferenced dir is reclaimed only once its owning gateway is gone — pid dead (`process.kill(pid, 0)`), or boot id changed by a reboot. Unmarked legacy dirs keep the prior age+liveness rule so pre-existing leaks are still swept, and a marker write failure is non-fatal (falls back to legacy), so ownership can never over-protect a leak. The primary case (gateway death with runs in flight, #105641) is unchanged: the dead gateway's pid fails the liveness probe, so the orphan is still removed.

Local validation on the rebased head (`5bf9437d`): `oxlint` clean, `tsgo:core` + `tsgo:core:test` clean, `check:temp-path-guardrails` pass, `deadcode:exports` adds no new entry (the marker name is module-private), and the `bundle-mcp-sweep` + `server-startup-post-attach` + `prepare` suites pass (217 tests).

## Tests

New `bundle-mcp-sweep.test.ts` covers the scenarios called out in the issue: gateway death with runs in flight (orphan removed), a live CLI child keeping its dir (#73244 control), a concurrent gateway instance's child keeping its dir, spawn-grace window, fail-closed on empty process scan, legacy empty dirs, and non-matching entries/missing roots. Owner-aware cases added: a queued run whose owning gateway is still alive is kept, a dead-owner dir is removed, a dir whose owner boot id predates a reboot is removed even if the pid was reused, and a live-owned dir with a matching boot id is kept.

`server-startup-post-attach.test.ts` mocks the sweep module so the existing startup test doesn't touch the real tmpdir/process table; its assertions are unchanged.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

https://claude.ai/code/session_01TiH8Npb28iWm4ZkXVrN4HJ

target.title: fix(skills): globally installed ClawHub skills falsely show as not tracked [AI-assisted]
target.body:
> [AI-assisted] This PR was generated using Claude Code.

Closes #105530

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users who install a ClawHub skill globally (`openclaw skills install <slug> --global`) see the skill flagged as `ClawHub link invalid` in the skill list, with the message:

> Skill `<slug>` has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile.

The skill is in fact correctly installed and tracked - but in the **global** lockfile (`~/.openclaw/.clawhub/lock.json`, i.e. `CONFIG_DIR/.clawhub/lock.json`), not the workspace lockfile. The status check only consulted the workspace lockfile, so every globally installed skill false-positive'd as invalid.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` read a single ClawHub lockfile (the workspace's) and passed it to every skill's linkage resolver, including skills installed under the managed/global skills directory (`CONFIG_DIR/skills`). It also passed the workspace dir as the expected-install-dir base, so a managed skill (installed at `CONFIG_DIR/skills/<slug>`) could never match the expected `workspaceDir/skills/<slug>`.

The fix resolves each skill's ClawHub linkage against its **owning install scope**:

- a skill under `managedSkillsDir` (a `--global` install) is checked against the managed lockfile at `dirname(managedSkillsDir)/.clawhub/lock.json` (i.e. `CONFIG_DIR/.clawhub/lock.json`), with the managed dir as the expected install root;
- a skill under the workspace `skills/` dir keeps the existing workspace-lockfile + workspace-install-root behavior.

The resolver (`resolveClawHubSkillStatusLinkSync`) is unchanged - the scope is selected at the single call site in `buildSkillStatus`, and the managed lockfile is read once in `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus`. Routing each scope to its own lockfile means identical slugs installed in both scopes cannot cross-link: a workspace skill only ever checks the workspace lockfile, a managed skill only ever checks the managed lockfile.

## User Impact

Globally installed ClawHub skills that are correctly tracked in the global lockfile now show as valid/linked in the skill list instead of being falsely flagged `ClawHub link invalid`. Workspace-scoped skills are unchanged.

## Evidence

Real behavior captured by driving the real `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` against an on-disk managed skill (`<managedRoot>/skills/weather-global/` with `.clawhub/origin.json`) plus a matching managed ClawHub lockfile (`<managedRoot>/.clawhub/lock.json`). The workspace has no ClawHub lockfile, mirroring a clean workspace with a `--global` install. Regression tests live in `src/skills/discovery/status-workspace.test.ts`.

**Before fix (current `main`)** - the managed skill is resolved against the (missing) workspace lockfile, so it false-positives as invalid. Actual `skill.clawhub` returned by `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus`:

```
status: "invalid"
valid: false
reason: "Skill \"weather-global\" has ClawHub origin metadata but is not tracked by the workspace ClawHub lockfile."
registry: "https://clawhub.example.com"
slug: "weather-global"
installedVersion: "1.0.0"
installedAt: 1700000000000
originPath: <managedRoot>/skills/weather-global/.clawhub/origin.json
(no lockPath - the workspace lockfile is missing)
```

**After fix** - the managed skill is resolved against its owning managed lockfile and links correctly. Actual `skill.clawhub` returned by `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus`:

```
status: "linked"
valid: true
registry: "https://clawhub.example.com"
slug: "weather-global"
installedVersion: "1.0.0"
installedAt: 1700000000000
originPath: <managedRoot>/skills/weather-global/.clawhub/origin.json
lockPath: <managedRoot>/.clawhub/lock.json
```

**Cross-scope isolation** (no cross-linking): a second regression test installs a managed skill whose slug also exists in the workspace lockfile. On `main`, the managed skill resolves against the workspace lockfile (`lockPath` = the workspace lockfile - wrong scope). After the fix, it resolves against the managed lockfile only (`lockPath` = the managed lockfile), staying `invalid` because the managed lockfile does not track it - it is never validated by the workspace lockfile's same-slug entry.

Local verification:

- `pnpm tsgo` (core prod types) - pass
- `oxlint` + `oxfmt --check` on changed files - pass
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/skills/discovery/status-workspace.test.ts` - 10/10 pass (both new regression tests fail on `main`, pass after the fix)
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/skills/discovery/status.test.ts src/skills/lifecycle/clawhub.test.ts` - 11 passed | 1 skipped (no regressions in the resolver's own suite)

Not tested: macOS/iOS skill discovery paths (Windows host); the live `openclaw skills list` UI (the proof drives the real `buildWorkspaceSkillStatus` function directly against a real on-disk managed install).
