target.title: Workspaces: add version history and exact restore
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Workspace operators had undo but no inspectable version history: they could not preview an older snapshot, understand structural changes, or restore the exact version they reviewed. The original #101900 implementation was built on the superseded Dashboard stack and retained race, corruption, attribution, and sparse-history correctness issues.

## Why This Change Was Made

This rebuild adds SQLite-backed history list/get/restore methods to the current Workspaces store and a history panel in the Workspaces UI. Restore is bound to the exact snapshot version the operator confirmed and executes inside the synchronous write transaction; the pre-restore workspace remains undoable and the resulting workspace version remains monotonic.

Corrupt rows are isolated instead of blocking valid older history. Change summaries use accurate creator/provenance terminology, distinguish move from resize, and report first-seen evidence as exact, bounded, or unknown when coverage is sparse. The UI documents the structural diff surface rather than claiming exhaustive content diffs.

The recovery also moves extension-owned synchronous SQLite queries through typed Kysely helpers exposed on the focused plugin-state SDK subpath.

## User Impact

- Operators can browse stored workspace versions and preview structural changes.
- Restore always targets the exact confirmed snapshot, even if another writer changes the workspace after preview.
- Damaged history rows do not hide or redirect valid restore choices.
- Restore failures keep the panel open and do not falsely present success.
- Current approval decisions remain protected from historical rollback.

## Evidence

- Rebased onto current `main` at `d287c9b414a`; the only conflict was the plugin SDK surface budget, reconciled to the exact three intentional helper exports.

target.title: Workspaces: add stream and computed bindings
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Workspaces could read one-shot RPC, file, and static values, but could not express live socket-backed values or safe client-side derivations. The original #101878 implementation was tied to the superseded Dashboard stack and left its new kinds inaccessible or ambiguous on current authoring surfaces.

## Why This Change Was Made

This rebuild ports only the binding-kind delta onto the Workspaces architecture landed by #104139. It adds allowlisted `stream` bindings, fixed-operation `computed` bindings, and an explicit `outputBinding` so rendering never depends on object insertion order.

The server returns the binding contract consumed by the UI, while the gateway seam has a real integration test to prevent drift. CLI and agent tools can author both kinds. Stream events are limited to channels visible to read-scoped clients (`presence` and `sessions.changed`); write-scoped workspace-change broadcasts are not advertised. Computed expressions use a closed operation switch and may reference only validated non-computed, non-stream sibling inputs.

## User Impact

- Workspace widgets can update from approved live events without polling when a readable event exists.
- Widgets can derive sums, averages, minimums, maximums, counts, last values, JSON-pointer picks, and fixed-format output without `eval` or arbitrary code.
- Multiple bindings require an explicit output, and existing multi-binding documents migrate their prior first-binding choice once.
- Poll and refetch cycles preserve current stream values instead of blanking the widget.

## Evidence

- Rebased onto current `main` at `d287c9b414a` with one reviewed schema conflict: upstream removed an unused migration helper, while this feature now uses it for the required one-time `outputBinding` migration.
- Post-rebase focused Vitest: 9 files, 118 tests passed across schema, migration/store, data reads, CLI, tools, gateway contract, UI normalization, and workspace rendering.
- Extension test TypeScript passed before the final rebase; the rebase changed only the migration-helper conflict and the complete post-rebase suite is green.
- Scoped formatting and `git diff --check` passed.
- Repository autoreview: clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- No GitNexus refresh or reset was performed.

Closes #101150.

target.title: fix(config): apply provider-level contextWindow/maxTokens defaults to models
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #105803.

`ModelProviderConfig` exposes `contextWindow`, `contextTokens`, and `maxTokens` as provider-level defaults, and the docs say they should act as defaults for models under that provider. However, `applyModelDefaults` in `src/config/defaults.ts` only looked at per-model values and never read the provider-level fields. As a result, users who set these fields at the provider level saw them silently ignored and replaced with the global defaults.

This is a follow-up gap to #44786, which fixed the runtime/discovered-model path.

## Why This Change Was Made

The config-loading path now mirrors the documented precedence: **per-model > provider-level > global default**. The change is minimal:

- Read `provider.contextWindow`, `provider.contextTokens`, and `provider.maxTokens` once per provider.
- Use them as fallbacks when a model entry omits the corresponding field.
- Keep existing clamping behavior: inherited `maxTokens` is still capped by the effective `contextWindow` and by provider-specific safe caps such as the Mistral safe maximum.

## User Impact

Users configuring OpenAI-compatible proxies or local providers (e.g. Ollama) can now set `contextWindow`/`contextTokens`/`maxTokens` once at the provider level instead of repeating them on every model entry. Per-model overrides continue to work exactly as before.

## Evidence

### Unit tests

Added regression tests in `src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts`:

- `falls back to provider-level contextWindow and maxTokens when a model omits them`
- `lets per-model contextWindow and maxTokens override provider-level defaults`
- `clamps provider-level maxTokens to provider-level contextWindow`
- `propagates provider-level contextTokens default to models`
- `lets per-model contextTokens override provider-level default`

All new and existing tests pass:

```
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
  src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts \
  src/config/defaults.test.ts \
  src/commands/doctor-legacy-config.migrations.test.ts
```

Result: 94 tests passed (23 + 8 + 63).

### Real configuration-loading transcript

The script below exercises the actual `applyModelDefaults` path with a redacted OpenAI-compatible proxy configuration:

```ts
// proof-provider-defaults.mts
import { applyModelDefaults } from "./src/config/defaults.js";

const cfg = {
  models: {
    providers: {
      myproxy: {
        baseUrl: "https://proxy.example.com/v1",        // redacted
        apiKey: "sk-xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",   // redacted
        api: "openai-completions",
        contextWindow: 50_000,
        contextTokens: 32_000,
        maxTokens: 4_096,
        models: [{ id: "gpt-5.4", name: "GPT-5.4 via proxy",
                   reasoning: false, input: ["text"],
                   cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 } }],
      },
    },
  },
} as never;

console.log(applyModelDefaults(cfg).models?.providers?.myproxy?.models?.[0]);
```

Run with `node_modules/.bin/tsx proof-provider-defaults.mts`:

```
Case 1: model omits limits -> inherits provider defaults
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 50000,
  contextTokens: 32000,
  maxTokens: 4096,
  ...
}

Case 2: per-model limits override provider defaults
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 10000,
  contextTokens: 8000,
  maxTokens: 2048,
  ...
}

Case 3: provider maxTokens clamped to provider contextWindow
{
  id: 'gpt-5.4',
  contextWindow: 4096,
  contextTokens: 4000,
  maxTokens: 4096,
  ...
}
```

Before the fix, Case 1 produced `contextWindow: 200000`, `contextTokens: undefined`, and `maxTokens: 8192` (the global defaults). After the fix, all three provider-level values are inherited as documented.

target.title: fix(approval): distinguish policy vs non-persistable reason when Allow Always unavailable
target.body:
Fixes #97069.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running commands with shell redirection (e.g. `openclaw --version 2>&1`) would see "The effective approval policy requires approval every time, so Allow Always is unavailable" — even when their effective policy is `ask=on-miss`. All nine approval prompt renderers (reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, and gateway API) blamed the policy instead of the real cause: the command is non-persistable and cannot be saved as an allow-always rule.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveExecApprovalAllowedDecisions()` returns the same `["allow-once", "deny"]` for both `ask=always` (policy) and one-shot persistence (non-persistable command). Downstream renderers had no way to distinguish the two cases.

Rather than introducing a new typed protocol field (which previous attempts attempted across 65+ files), we thread the existing `ask` field — already present in the request payload, approval view, and gateway pipeline — through the approval-pending data pipeline so renderers can branch on it. Approval policy logic is unchanged.

The `node` host path uses `approvalDecisionAsk` (`maxAsk(hostAsk, nodeAsk)`) to keep the reasoning consistent with `allowedDecisions` computation even when the node policy is stricter than the host policy.

## User Impact

Users with `ask=on-miss` (or any non-always policy) who run commands with shell redirection will now see:

> Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted (e.g., shell redirection or dynamic content).

Instead of the misleading policy message. Users with `ask=always` see the same policy message as before. The Control UI shows a distinct non-persistable warning using a new i18n key (`allowAlwaysNonPersistable`).

| `ask` input | Message shown |
|---|---|
| `"always"` | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" |
| `"on-miss"` (one-shot) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| `"off"` (shell redirect) | "Allow Always is unavailable because this command cannot be persisted…" |
| absent / null | "The effective approval policy requires approval every time…" (safe default) |

## Evidence

**18 files, +109/−23 lines.** Core logic is 52 lines; tests add 57 lines.

**Renderers fixed (all 9):** reply, forwarder, agent-facing, Control UI, reaction, embedded handler, Telegram handler, Telegram forwarding, gateway API error message.

**Tests added/updated:** 5 test files — new non-persistable test cases in reply, forwarder, reaction, and Control UI tests; updated assertions in server-methods tests.

**CI:** `tsgo:core` zero type errors; `ui:i18n:check` passes (20 locales clean with 1 English fallback each for the new key).

target.title: fix(agents): decouple MCP retirement from browser cleanup
target.body:
Related: #76233
Related: #101830

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a completed run-mode subagent waits for sequential browser-tab cleanup before retiring its bundle MCP runtime and starting completion delivery. A browser close request can wait up to the browser service timeout per tab, so one run with several tabs can delay MCP retirement, the completion announcement, and the next same-session turn.

The concrete browser-cleanup delay is separate from the MCP lease-disposal race covered by #76233 and the related #101830 work.

## Why This Change Was Made

Browser cleanup is dispatched as independent owner-scoped work, while MCP retirement and completion announcement proceed after the existing generation and lease-safety checks. Browser operations hold a per-session access gate for their full request; cleanup takes the exclusive gate, so a successor browser turn waits safely instead of racing an already-issued close request.

The browser registry tracks the opaque run owner and an ordered ownership claim. Successor reuse transfers ownership; late predecessor callbacks cannot reclaim or remove the successor tab. Failed non-ignorable closes remain tracked for a later cleanup, and legacy unowned tabs remain eligible for cleanup.

## User Impact

Run-mode subagent completion no longer waits for the browser service to close every tracked tab before MCP retirement and completion delivery begin. A successor turn can start its non-browser work immediately and its browser work is admitted after the old cleanup gate releases, preserving tab safety. App-view MCP leases continue to defer retirement until their release path completes.

## Evidence

- Deterministic browser registry barriers: 13 tests pass, covering active access vs. exclusive cleanup, successor blocking, owner transfer, late predecessor callbacks, blocked aliases, failed-close retry, legacy tabs, and idle sweeps.
- Browser tool regression suite: 91 tests pass, including full-request access gating and run-owner propagation.
- Lifecycle/context regression suites: 88 lifecycle tests and 107 lifecycle/context tests pass; the lifecycle barrier verifies MCP retirement and announcement start while browser cleanup remains unresolved, and successor generation cleanup verifies that old browser cleanup is dispatched without retiring the successor MCP runtime.
- Browser lifecycle cleanup unit suite: 4 tests pass.
- SDK surface check passed: `node scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.mjs --check`.
- Formatting and lint passed for the touched extension and core scopes (`oxfmt`, `run-oxlint.mjs` with the repository configs); `git diff --check` passed.

The approved Crabbox/Testbox backend was unavailable because this environment had no usable AWS credentials, so focused validation used the repository's narrow local Vitest fallback. One broader local sibling batch had an existing MCP subprocess timing test fail only in the full batch; its isolated retry passed, while the other sibling suites passed.

target.title: fix(gateway): count pending restarts toward maxRestartsPerHour budget
target.body:
### What Problem This Solves
close #105189
When a channel is permanently stuck in a pending restart state, two issues arise:

1. **Budget bypass**: The health monitor skips the maxRestartsPerHour check for pending restarts, causing infinite restart attempts.
2. **No completion pass**: Even after counting pending restarts toward the hourly budget, a recovery that consumed the last slot cannot finish — it hits the cap on the next tick.
3. **Rollover starvation**: After the completion pass is exhausted, old restart records eventually fall out of the 1-hour window — but `completionPassAllowed` stays `true`, silently starving the channel forever.

### Why This Change Was Made

Issue 1: The `continuingPendingRestart` guard prevented both the rate-limit check and the restart record update for pending restarts. Once a channel entered a permanently-pending state, every monitor tick would attempt another restart without counting it against the hourly budget.

Issue 2: With the cap applied uniformly, a pending recovery that used the last hourly slot would be blocked on the very next check, preventing it from ever completing.

Issue 3 (rollover): `completionPassAllowed` is set to `true` once the completion pass is granted, and only reset when a new restart record is pushed. After the hourly window rolls over and old records are pruned, the flag remains `true`, so the channel is stuck with zero budget — even though capacity has reopened.

### What Changed

- Pending restarts count toward `maxRestartsPerHour` — the rate limit guard no longer skips for pending restarts
- Pending restarts are recorded in `restartsThisHour` — the record update no longer skips for pending restarts
- **One completion pass**: When a pending recovery hits the hourly cap, it gets one extra pass to finish, without pushing a new restart record. A `completionPassAllowed` flag tracks this — reset on each new restart record
- **Rollover reset**: `pruneOldRestarts` now resets `completionPassAllowed` when pruning old entries reopens budget capacity (`before >= maxRestarts && after < maxRestarts`)
- The cooldown check (fresh-restart throttle) still correctly skips for pending restarts, since they continue an already-begun recovery

### Evidence

#### Regression Tests

`src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.test.ts:569` — caps pending recovery restarts at the configured maxRestartsPerHour with one completion pass: Simulates a channel where every restart transitions to pending, configures maxRestartsPerHour=2, runs 30 seconds of health checks, and asserts startChannel is called exactly 3 times (2 budgeted + 1 completion pass).

`src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.test.ts:607` — grants one completion pass for a pending recovery that consumed the last hourly slot: Tick-by-tick verification proving the completion pass is exactly one.

`src/gateway/channel-health-monitor.test.ts:945` — resets completion-pass flag when pruning reopens hourly budget: Exhausts budget (3 calls), confirms capped, then advances time just past the 1-hour prune point. Proves the first post-rollover pending attempt consumes a fresh budget slot (call 4 → 5 → 6 with completion pass), then caps again.

`src/gateway/live-rollover.test.ts` — continuous, timestamped, redacted gateway log capture covering the full lifecycle across one hourly rollover boundary (see output below).

#### Test Output

```
 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  188 passed (188)
```

#### Live Gateway Logs — Scenario 1: Normal pending recovery completes

```
[health-monitor] started
[health-monitor] [whatsapp:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: disconnected)
[health-monitor] [whatsapp:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)
```
→ 2 calls. Channel recovered. Budget (5) not exhausted.

#### Live Gateway Logs — Scenario 2: Permanent pending retries cap correctly

```
[health-monitor] started
[health-monitor] [discord:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: disconnected)    ← slot 1/2
[health-monitor] [discord:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)         ← slot 2/2
[health-monitor] [discord:default] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)         ← completion pass
[health-monitor] [discord:default] health-monitor: hit 2 restarts/hour limit, skipping  ← capped
  ... (repeated 4×)
```

#### Live Gateway Logs — Scenario 3: Continuous rollover lifecycle (full hour)

Continuous, timestamped, redacted test output covering the capped state → 1-hour rollover → renewed attempts → completion pass → second cap:

```
[health-monitor] started (interval: 0s, startup-grace: 0s, channel-connect-grace: 120s)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: disconnected)   ← call #1 (initial)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)        ← call #2 (slot 2/2)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)        ← call #3 (completion pass)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: hit 2 restarts/hour limit, skipping ← CAP #1
  ... ~35,940 skipped (capped) across 1-hour window ...

  *** ~1 hour passes — pruneOldRestarts reopens budget ***

[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)        ← call #4 (rollover, budget reopened)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)        ← call #5 (slot 2/2 in new window)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: restarting (reason: stopped)        ← call #6 (completion pass in new window)
[health-monitor] [dummy:main] health-monitor: hit 2 restarts/hour limit, skipping ← CAP #2 (after rollover)
  ... ~35,940 skipped (capped) ...
```

**Lifecycle**: calls 1–3 exhaust the first hourly budget (2 slots + 1 completion pass), then ~35,940 health checks skip while capped. After `pruneOldRestarts` removes records older than 1 hour, the budget reopens: calls 4–6 repeat the same pattern (2 slots + 1 completion pass) in the fresh 1-hour window. After call 6, the second cap activates — the channel is again rate-limited.

target.title: feat(nodes): continue Claude catalog sessions on paired nodes via streaming CLI agent runs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Claude Code catalog sessions on paired nodes were view-only: `continueClaudeSession` rejected any `hostId` other than `gateway:local`, so a session whose files live on another machine could be browsed but never continued. Closes #105529.

## Why This Change Was Made

Continuing a Claude session must run the real `claude` CLI on the machine that owns the session files (its `~/.claude`, its auth) — OpenClaw stays a frontend and never substitutes its own inference. This PR ships the full TS stack for that, opt-in and approval-gated end to end:

- **Streaming node invoke (additive transport)**: new `node.invoke.progress` events (`{invokeId, nodeId, seq, chunk}`) with strict seq ordering, bounded out-of-order buffering, idle-timeout reset on progress, hard-cap timeout, and `node.invoke.cancel`. Legacy single-result invokes stay byte-identical (cancel frames are gated to streaming invokes). Progress handlers are node-scoped and bind invokeId to the owning node's connection — no cross-node injection.
- **Node command `agent.cli.claude.run.v1`** (TS node host): advertised only when the node-local config `nodeHost.agentRuns.claude.enabled` is true AND the `claude` binary resolves on the node — the gateway can never force it on. Requests are validated against a strict Claude flag allowlist (`bypassPermissions` rejected in both arg forms), env passthrough is allowlisted, cwd must exist, and every run flows through the existing `system.run` exec-approval policy with the exact validated argv. Output is capped (200KB, 16KB chunks with backpressure), stderr tailed, process tree SIGKILLed on cancel/timeout, and the system prompt is materialized in a node-local 0600 temp file that is always cleaned up.
- **cli-runner placement branch**: sessions with `execHost === "node"` run one-shot `claude -p` turns through the streaming invoke, feeding the same JSONL parser as local runs (session-id capture, fork markers, tool events unchanged). Warm stdio, gateway-loopback MCP, skills dirs, reseed-from-transcript, and attachments are cleanly disabled for node runs (rejected or omitted, double-enforced by the node-side allowlist); local runs are byte-identical.
- **Catalog wiring**: node rows become continuable when the node advertises the run command AND the gateway's node command policy permits it (deny-wins, enforced at projection, continue, and invoke time). Adoption re-resolves the record from the node itself (client-supplied paths never trusted), imports bounded history via the existing read command, and binds the session with `execNode`/`execCwd` through the trusted creation seam. First-turn `--fork-session` semantics identical to local adoption.

Mac-app (Swift) nodes simply never advertise the command and remain view-only until the app ships it.

## User Impact

With a headless node host opted in (`nodeHost.agentRuns.claude.enabled: true` + `claude` installed), Claude Code sessions on that machine appear in the session catalog and can be continued like native sessions: each turn runs on the node with the node's Claude auth and settings, streams output live, and respects the node's exec approval policy. Nothing changes for nodes that do not opt in; existing node/gateway deployments see zero wire-format changes.

## Evidence

- Focused matrix green post-rebase (8 Vitest shards): node-registry transport ordering/idle/disconnect, node-host argv-validation/approval/caps/cancel, cli-runner placement/JSONL-across-chunks/fork/deadline-during-approval, config contract, plugin runtime projection, catalog adoption/rejection paths.
- Codex-side validation on Linux Testbox: 12 test files (574 executions), `check:changed` (12m21s), `pnpm build` — all green pre-review.
- Three independent deep reviews (transport, cli-runner placement, catalog/config/plugin seams): all SOLID, zero P1s. The one P2 (hard-timeout previously emitted `node.invoke.cancel` for legacy invokes too) is fixed — cancel frames now gate on the streaming contract.
- Per-commit autoreview (gpt-5.6-sol xhigh) surfaced five findings, all fixed with regression tests: buffered progress no longer drains after cancellation; duplicate buffered seq frames no longer reset the idle deadline; node runs now carry the gateway's native tool policy (`--tools` + MCP deny projected; `--allowedTools` auto-approval still never crosses the node boundary); fresh node CLI sessions reseed conversation history from the gateway-side transcript; and a truncated node stream that lost the terminal result line now fails the turn instead of passing as a clean exit.
- SDK gates: `plugin-sdk:api:check` and `plugin-sdk:surface:check` green (surface budget +1 for `resolveChildProcessInvocation`, now public via the `process-runtime` wildcard — needed by the node host for Windows shim-correct spawns).
- tsgo core + UI lanes green; oxlint/oxfmt/`git diff --check` clean.

Known follow-ups (deliberate v1 scope, in the tracking issue): Mac-app Swift command, warm stdio on nodes, gateway-loopback MCP over node transport, Codex app-server on nodes, approval-request withdrawal when a run aborts mid-wait, FailoverError classification for node disconnects.

target.title: fix(gateway): add base64 validation before decode in persistInboundImagesForTranscript
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `persistInboundImagesForTranscript` in `chat-attachments.ts` decodes base64 image data via `Buffer.from(image.data, "base64")` without validating the format first. The same file already has an `isValidBase64` utility used in another code path (line 349), but this path lacks the pre-check. Invalid base64 could silently produce empty/malformed buffers.

**Solution**: Add `isValidBase64` pre-check before `Buffer.from(image.data, "base64")`, reusing the existing utility in the same file. The check throws on invalid base64, which is caught by the existing try-catch wrapper and logged as a warning.

**What changed**: One `if (!isValidBase64(...))` guard added in `persistInboundImagesForTranscript`. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — scoped addition of format validation to an existing inbound path, reusing a tested utility defined in the same file. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Invalid base64 image data is now rejected with a clear error before Buffer.from decode, instead of silently producing an empty/malformed buffer.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0

**After-fix evidence**: TypeScript compilation succeeds. `isValidBase64` is already used in the same file (line 349), and the pre-check integrates cleanly into the existing try-catch flow.

**Observed result after the fix**: Build passes cleanly. Invalid base64 inputs will throw before buffer decode; valid inputs pass through unchanged.

**What was not tested**: End-to-end image upload scenario through the Gateway runtime.

- `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0 ✓

- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — built successfully with default config
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal validation guard
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.title: fix(agents): tighten grepSchema context/limit from Type.Number to Type.Integer
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `grepSchema.context` and `grepSchema.limit` in `src/agents/sessions/tools/grep.ts` accept floating-point values via `Type.Number()`, while both fields represent integer semantics — context lines and match count. A float value (e.g. `context=1.5`) could silently truncate, giving unexpected results.

**Solution**: Tighten both `context` and `limit` to `Type.Integer()` — matching the pattern already applied to sibling tool schemas (`read.ts`, `find.ts`, `ls.ts`). TypeBox rejects float values at the parameter parsing stage.

**What changed**: Two `Type.Number()` → `Type.Integer()` replacements in `grep.ts`. No runtime logic changes. No config, CLI, or public API surface changed.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — schema-only change to an internal tool schema type. No session state, auth, message delivery, or security boundary involved.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Schema-level rejection of float values for `context` and `limit` in the grep tool. Type.Integer enforces integer-only input at parameter parsing time.

**Real environment tested**: Linux x86_64 (local workstation)

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0

**After-fix evidence**: TypeScript compilation succeeds with the updated schema types. The `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` target confirms the source is syntactically and semantically valid.

**Observed result after the fix**: Build passes cleanly. The schema change is validated at compile time (Type.Integer is a valid TypeBox schema type accepted by TypeScript's type checker).

**What was not tested**: End-to-end LLM grep tool invocation through the Gateway runtime. The schema type change compiles and is type-safe; runtime behavior change (float rejection) is enforced by TypeBox's Value.Check at tool-call time.

## Tests and validation

- `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` → exit 0 ✓ (compilation succeeds with updated schema type)

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible — existing callers passing integer values work identically; callers passing floats now get a clear validation error at schema level
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations — built successfully with default config
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation — not needed, internal tool schema change
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary — no breaking changes

target.title: feat(memory): add multi-slot memory role architecture
target.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a memory-plugin architecture flaw: OpenClaw currently has one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner even though the product, docs, bundled plugins, and runtime behavior already treat “memory” as several different responsibilities.

Today, factual recall, auto-capture, compaction, dreaming/consolidation, and user/session modeling are all forced through the same global selector. That makes documented memory stacks impossible or brittle: selecting one memory provider can unintentionally displace another provider that owns a different responsibility.

This PR corrects that mismatch by introducing purpose-specific memory role slots:

- `memory.recall`
- `memory.capture`
- `memory.compaction`
- `memory.dreaming`
- `memory.userModel`

The new role slots are the mechanism. The fix is that OpenClaw can now represent the memory architecture it already documents and partially implements.

## What Problem This Solves

This is a flaw fix, not just a feature request.

OpenClaw’s memory ecosystem is already multi-role:

- `memory-core` / QMD provide local factual recall/search over project memory, session transcripts, and Markdown/QMD corpora.
- Honcho provides cross-session user, agent, and session modeling.
- LanceDB provides embedding-backed long-term recall and auto-capture.
- Active Memory orchestrates recall before generation by using whichever provider owns recall.
- Memory Wiki compiles durable memory into a companion knowledge vault rather than replacing active memory.
- Dreaming/consolidation is a separate runtime responsibility from ordinary recall.

The current `plugins.slots.memory` contract cannot express that architecture. It treats every `kind: "memory"` provider as competing for one owner slot, even when the providers are designed to do different jobs. That leads to three concrete problems:

1. **Documented combinations are not representable.** Configs such as builtin/QMD recall + Honcho user modeling, LanceDB capture + local recall, or Active Memory over a selected recall provider cannot be modeled cleanly through one memory owner.
2. **Runtime behavior depends on exceptions and side paths.** Plugins that should compose have to rely on context-engine ownership, sidecar behavior, fallback logic, or plugin-specific handling instead of a shared contract.
3. **Diagnostics and lifecycle handling become misleading.** Startup, validation, status, doctor repair, skill publishing, uninstall cleanup, runtime memory resolution, and SDK-facing aliases need to know which provider owns which memory responsibility.

So while this PR adds new public config keys, the intent is corrective: make the config/runtime contract match the memory system OpenClaw already exposes.

## User Impact / Intended Outcome

After this PR, OpenClaw can express memory stacks that were previously documented or implied but not cleanly configurable:

- `memory-core` or QMD can own factual recall while Honcho owns user/session modeling.
- LanceDB can own recall and/or capture without forcing unrelated memory roles through the same selector.
- Active Memory can use the configured `memory.recall` provider instead of depending on hard-coded assumptions.
- Dreaming/consolidation can be selected separately from ordinary recall where supported.
- Memory Wiki can remain a companion compiled-knowledge layer beside active memory providers.
- Existing configs using `plugins.slots.memory` continue to work as recall selection.
- `openclaw doctor --fix` can migrate/canonicalize non-conflicting legacy memory-slot config while preserving the legacy key for plugin compatibility.

## Linked Context

Closes #60572.

Directly related memory-composition requests and prior proposals:

- #38874: supplementary/additive memory plugins alongside the primary memory slot.
- #2306: earlier closed PR proposing stackable memory plugins.
- #2080: earlier request for multiple simultaneous memory plugins and emerging memory architectures.
- #77714: pluggable persistent memory backend demand.

Dreaming and memory-role separation context:

- #85473: future protocol work for making dreaming implementable by non-`memory-core` memory plugins. This PR adds the `memory.dreaming` slot contract but does not implement that full protocol.
- #63067 and #65411: prior work around keeping dreaming behavior available when another plugin owns the legacy memory slot.
- #62275: previous selected-slot dreaming config behavior.

Runtime/diagnostic slot handling context:

- #76567 and #76495: configured memory-slot runtime checks should load/consult the selected memory plugin.
- #78540: doctor/status memory diagnostics could misreport configured memory providers.
- #76550: stale `plugins.slots.*` references could leave config unrecoverable until doctor cleanup was broadened.

Context-engine compatibility context:

- #77063, #77185, #76576, and #81843: context-engine registration and LosslessClaw-adjacent failures shaped the compatibility review for preserving the existing global `plugins.slots.contextEngine` behavior while rejecting unsupported per-agent `contextEngine` config.

Future API/RFC context:

- #70823: future machine-readable slot ownership/provenance. This PR intentionally keeps scalar plugin IDs and solves the memory role composition layer first.

Memory-plugin interop research: the [supporting research document](https://github.com/kklouzal/rfcs/blob/rfc/multi-slot-memory-role-architecture/rfcs/0009/memory-plugin-interop-research.md) validates this PR as necessary architecture work, not optional extensibility: OpenClaw's own documentation already describes memory as a composable ecosystem where builtin/QMD recall, Honcho user/session modeling, LanceDB recall/capture, Active Memory orchestration, dreaming/consolidation, and Memory Wiki compilation can coexist, but current `origin/main` collapses every `kind: "memory"` provider into one exclusive `plugins.slots.memory` owner, making those documented combinations impossible or dependent on brittle exceptions. PR #88504 closes that product/docs/runtime gap by replacing the single memory owner with explicit role slots — `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel` — while preserving legacy `memory` as a recall shorthand, so the documented memory-plugin interop story becomes actually representable in config and runtime behavior.

## What Changes

- Adds canonical memory role slots: `memory.recall`, `memory.capture`, `memory.compaction`, `memory.dreaming`, and `memory.userModel`.
- Keeps legacy `plugins.slots.memory` as a backward-compatible shorthand for `memory.recall` during an extended migration window.
- Adds per-agent memory role-slot overrides under `agents.list[*].plugins.slots`, limited to memory roles plus legacy `memory`.
- Wires role-slot selection through config schema/types/help/docs, plugin activation, gateway startup preloading, runtime memory resolution, skill publishing, validation, doctor repair/preview, uninstall cleanup, status diagnostics, and SDK-facing aliases.
- Preserves the existing global `plugins.slots.contextEngine` path for LosslessClaw and other context-engine plugins.
- Explicitly rejects unsupported per-agent `agents.list[*].plugins.slots.contextEngine` overrides because agent-scoped context-engine semantics are outside this PR.

## Implementation Notes

- Adds `src/plugins/slot-resolution.ts` as the shared role-slot helper layer for canonical memory role keys, defaults, normalization, effective per-agent resolution, and configured selection collection.
- Updates config schema/types/help/labels/docs for global and per-agent memory role slots.
- Keeps `PluginSlotsConfig.contextEngine` for global plugin slots, and adds an agent-slot type/schema that omits `contextEngine`.
- Updates doctor legacy memory-slot handling so `doctor --fix` canonicalizes to `memory.recall` while retaining legacy `memory` during the compatibility window.
- Updates plugin loader/activation/startup resolution so explicit role-slot selections activate memory plugins without confusing default `memory-core` fallback with a user-selected plugin under restrictive allowlists.
- Extends validation to report missing role-slot plugin refs and validate schemas for plugins selected only by non-recall or per-agent memory roles.
- Extends skill publishing, status scanning, uninstall cleanup, memory runtime, dreaming, compaction provider, and SDK alias behavior to use the role-aware model.
- Keeps memory runtime registrations addressable by plugin id, so runtime recall dispatch follows the resolved global or per-agent `memory.recall` owner.
- Passes the session agent id into Pi embedded extension factory construction so safeguard compaction provider selection honors per-agent `memory.compaction` overrides in both normal session runs and manual/queued compaction paths.
- Updates bundled memory plugin manifests/docs to describe role support and the recall shorthand migration.

target.title: fix(github-copilot): reject unsupported OAuth enterprise domain before refresh and model routing
target.body:
## Summary
A legacy `github-copilot` OAuth profile can carry an `enterpriseUrl` that is not a GitHub Copilot host. Current `main` templates that persisted value straight into the endpoint it sends the bearer credential to. The refresh path sends the refresh token to `api.<persisted-domain>`, and the model-routing path derives the completions base URL from the same credential, so an unexpired credential keeps routing its access token to that origin without ever reaching a refresh. No allowlist is applied on either path.

This rejects an off-allowlist persisted origin before a request is issued and before a model URL is produced.

## Root cause
`src/llm/utils/oauth/github-copilot.ts`. Two egress points, both reachable from persisted state.

Refresh, before:

```ts
export async function refreshGitHubCopilotToken(refreshToken: string, enterpriseDomain?: string) {
  const domain = enterpriseDomain || "github.com";
  const urls = getUrls(domain);
  const raw = await fetchJson(urls.copilotTokenUrl, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${refreshToken}`, ...COPILOT_HEADERS },
  });
```

Model routing, before:

```ts
modifyModels(models: Model[], credentials: OAuthCredentials): Model[] {
  const creds = credentials as CopilotCredentials;
  const domain = creds.enterpriseUrl ? (normalizeDomain(creds.enterpriseUrl) ?? undefined) : undefined;
  const baseUrl = getGitHubCopilotBaseUrl(creds.access, domain);
  return models.map((m) => (m.provider === "github-copilot" ? { ...m, baseUrl } : m));
}
```

`normalizeDomain` only parses a hostname, it does not check one. `refreshToken` and `modifyModels` are both live on current `main`: `src/llm/utils/oauth/index.ts` registers `githubCopilotOAuthProvider` in the built-in OAuth registry, `oauth/index.ts:107` calls `provider.refreshToken(creds)`, and `src/agents/sessions/model-registry.ts:392-395` calls `oauthProvider.modifyModels(combined, cred)` for every `oauth` credential.

## Fix
An off-allowlist origin means the stored access token may itself have been minted by that origin, so its `proxy-ep` is not trustworthy either. The credential is therefore refused as a whole rather than coerced onto `github.com`, which would present an enterprise-scoped token to the wrong GitHub origin.

```ts
export function getGitHubCopilotBaseUrl(token?: string, enterpriseDomain?: string): string {
  if (enterpriseDomain && !isSupportedGithubCopilotDomain(enterpriseDomain)) {
    throw new Error(`Refusing to route GitHub Copilot requests for unsupported enterprise domain "${enterpriseDomain}". ...`);
  }
  ...
}

modifyModels(models: Model[], credentials: OAuthCredentials): Model[] {
  const creds = credentials as CopilotCredentials;
  if (!isSupportedGithubCopilotDomain(creds.enterpriseUrl)) {
    return models.filter((m) => m.provider !== "github-copilot");
  }
  const baseUrl = getGitHubCopilotBaseUrl(creds.access, creds.enterpriseUrl);
  return models.map((m) => (m.provider === "github-copilot" ? { ...m, baseUrl } : m));
}
```

`modifyModels` withholds the models rather than throwing, because it runs inside the model-registry loop for every provider and a throw there would break the whole model list. Withholding leaves the access token with no route. `refreshGitHubCopilotToken` rejects before issuing a request, `loginGitHubCopilot` rejects an unsupported host up front, and `formatAuthDoctorHint` points affected users at re-authentication, mirroring the existing qwen-portal hint.

## Why this is the right boundary
Every path that turns a persisted or user-supplied domain into a bearer-bearing URL now validates first: login, refresh, and model routing. Supported hosts are unchanged, `github.com` and `*.ghe.com` data-residency tenants still route and refresh exactly as before, so the compatibility cost falls only on credentials whose origin was never a Copilot host.

Rebased onto current `main`, which moved GitHub Copilot into `extensions/github-copilot`. That plugin owns a `token`-type profile and is a different credential shape; it already resolves its host through the SDK allowlist. The legacy `oauth`-type profile path fixed here is still registered and executable on `main` (the proof below resolves it through the real registry), so this is not obsolete code and the plugin does not already cover it. The allowlist and the new `isSupportedGithubCopilotDomain` predicate move to a dependency-free `plugin-sdk` leaf so the core OAuth runtime can share them without closing a module cycle; `plugin-sdk/provider-auth` re-exports `normalizeGithubCopilotDomain`, so `extensions/github-copilot/domain.ts` keeps its existing import unchanged.

A token's `proxy-ep` is still trusted when the minting origin is on the allowlist, which matches the plugin's own `deriveCopilotApiBaseUrlFromToken`. That trust is exactly what this patch withdraws when the origin is not on the allowlist.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/llm/utils/oauth/github-copilot.test.ts src/agents/auth-profiles.doctor.test.ts` passes, 31 tests. The 5 new domain and model-routing cases fail on pristine `main` (`copilot-api`/`api.attacker.example` produced, refresh resolves) and pass with the patch.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/github-copilot` is unchanged by this patch: 13 failed / 109 passed both on pristine `main` and with the patch, all in `extensions/github-copilot/index.test.ts` and unrelated to these files.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` and `oxfmt --check` clean on all 6 changed files.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json` clean; `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.core.test.json` reports no error in any changed file (pre-existing errors in `ui/src/components/mcp-app-view.ts` only).
- Full `pnpm build` not run.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a persisted github-copilot OAuth profile whose `enterpriseUrl` is not a Copilot host sends its bearer refresh token to that origin on refresh, and routes its access token to that origin during model use even when it never refreshes.
Real environment tested: the real built-in OAuth provider registry on pristine main afb282ee68 and on the patched tree at b85bd5db1f, resolved through `getOAuthProvider("github-copilot")` exactly as `oauth/index.ts` and `model-registry.ts` do, then driving the real `modifyModels` and `refreshToken` of `githubCopilotOAuthProvider`. The persisted credential, the registry, the provider, the allowlist and the doctor hint are all real; the only thing replaced is the outbound network boundary, a recording `fetch` that captures the URL and Authorization header instead of sending the credential to a real host. Scenarios B and C are unchanged controls.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: resolve `getOAuthProvider("github-copilot")` from the real registry, then for each persisted credential call `provider.modifyModels([gpt-5@github-copilot, claude-sonnet-5@anthropic], credential)` and `await provider.refreshToken(credential)`, recording every outbound request.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main afb282ee68)
registry lookup getOAuthProvider("github-copilot") -> GitHub Copilot

A. legacy profile minted by an off-allowlist host
  persisted enterpriseUrl: attacker.example
  model routing:  gpt-5 -> https://api.attacker.example
  token refresh:  completed
  requests carrying the credential: 1
    -> https://api.attacker.example/copilot_internal/v2/token   Bearer gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN

B. data-residency tenant (control)
  persisted enterpriseUrl: acme.ghe.com
  model routing:  gpt-5 -> https://api.acme.ghe.com
  token refresh:  completed
  requests carrying the credential: 1
    -> https://api.acme.ghe.com/copilot_internal/v2/token   Bearer gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN

C. public github.com profile (control)
  persisted enterpriseUrl: (none)
  model routing:  gpt-5 -> https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com
  token refresh:  completed
  requests carrying the credential: 1
    -> https://api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token   Bearer gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN

# AFTER (this patch, identical inputs)
registry lookup getOAuthProvider("github-copilot") -> GitHub Copilot

A. legacy profile minted by an off-allowlist host
  persisted enterpriseUrl: attacker.example
  model routing:  github-copilot withheld, access token has no route
  token refresh:  refused, Refusing to refresh GitHub Copilot token for unsupported enterprise domain "attacker.example". Re-authenticate with a supported host (github.com or a *.ghe.com tenant).
  requests carrying the credential: 0

B. data-residency tenant (control)
  persisted enterpriseUrl: acme.ghe.com
  model routing:  gpt-5 -> https://api.acme.ghe.com
  token refresh:  completed
  requests carrying the credential: 1
    -> https://api.acme.ghe.com/copilot_internal/v2/token   Bearer gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN

C. public github.com profile (control)
  persisted enterpriseUrl: (none)
  model routing:  gpt-5 -> https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com
  token refresh:  completed
  requests carrying the credential: 1
    -> https://api.github.com/copilot_internal/v2/token   Bearer gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN
```
Observed result after fix: on pristine main the off-allowlist profile hands `gho_VICTIM_REFRESH_TOKEN` to `api.attacker.example` and routes `gpt-5` to `https://api.attacker.example`, so the access token reaches that origin even with no refresh; after the patch that same profile issues zero outbound requests and its models are withheld entirely, while the `acme.ghe.com` tenant and the public `github.com` profile keep byte-identical routing and refresh behavior.
What was not tested: no live GitHub or Copilot request was made, the outbound boundary was recorded rather than sent, so no real credential left the process. Recovery is exercised at the doctor-hint and routing level rather than by running an interactive `openclaw onboard --auth-choice github-copilot` re-login end to end. Full `pnpm build` was not run.

target.title: feat(cloud-workers): openclaw worker mode running the embedded loop on the box
target.body:
Part of #104294 (cloud workers, milestone 2, PR 9 — the composition PR). Builds on the four landed milestone-2 backend contracts: #104688 (worker role), #104809 (transcript commits), #105275 (live events), #105719 (inference proxy). Design: `docs/plan/cloud-workers.md` (openclaw worker mode).

## What Problem This Solves

The four backend RPCs exist on the gateway side, but nothing yet runs an agent session ON a worker box. This PR adds `openclaw worker` mode: the entry point + worker-side runtime that dials the gateway over the reverse tunnel, admits with the minted credential + handshake, and runs the embedded agent loop on the box — with its persistence, model, and streaming seams tethered to the gateway, and tools running locally. This is where a worker box becomes capable of running a real session driven from the gateway.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `openclaw worker` entry: restricted runtime (loadPlugins:"never", no channels, no gateway HTTP surfaces, throwaway mkdtemp 0700 state dir, in-memory empty auth storage — no local model auth profile read). Dials the tunnel-forwarded local socket, presents credential + handshake, attaches to its single assigned session. Fails closed on admission failure (with a bounded 120s admission deadline so a leased box can't burn forever on an unreachable gateway).
- Embedded runner rewired: session persistence -> transcript-commit RPC client (base-leaf CAS + runEpoch + seq, durable replay dedupe); model calls -> inference-proxy RPC client (provider/model reference strings only, streamed deltas + terminal, durable-replay resume); streaming -> live-event RPC client (monotonic seq, cumulative ACK, unacked-tail replay). Tools are the six coding tools (read/write/edit/apply_patch/exec/process), local-only, fail-closed availability check.
- Reconnect/resume: exact-frame transcript retry (ledger dedupe), cumulative live-ACK replay of the unacked tail, durable inference resume (single provider call, no double-bill). Owner-epoch supersession -> clean fenced exit. Oversized transcript messages fail closed producer-side.

## Deep-review fixes (a dedicated adversarial review found real concurrency/lifecycle bugs)

- **BLOCKER fixed:** stop() during an in-flight transcript commit spun forever (100% CPU hang on SIGINT/SIGTERM) because the terminal `stopped` state was indistinguishable from a transient interrupt and the commit retry loop treated it as retryable. Introduced a terminal WorkerConnectionStoppedError; retry loops now retry only transient interruptions and rethrow on any terminal state. Stop-in-flight and post-stop emit settle promptly.
- **Blast-radius fixed:** a gateway live-event window reset (a streaming-telemetry cursor reset) used to abort the entire run including a healthy in-flight inference turn. Now: satisfiable resyncs renumber the unacked tail from the gateway's expectedSeq (the gateway explicitly tolerates renumbered replay); an unrecoverable live-seam failure degrades to lossy preview streaming while inference/transcript continue. Live events are preview; they no longer kill the turn.
- **Dead-seam removed + contract documented:** the unused in-process resumeFromBase resync was removed (leaf-only rebasing is unsafe — an unseen transcript mutation means stale inference context). On stale-base-leaf the run fail-stops with an explicit lost-tail lifecycle error and no duplicate commit; relaunch-with-fresh-context is milestone-3 (placement) territory, now documented in docs/cli/worker.md.
- **Hardening:** the worker's session write path is now a real promise-chain mutex (was a pass-through relying on an unguarded serial-emission invariant); bounded admission deadline.

## User Impact

Opt-in only; dispatch/UI (target bar, placement) is milestone 3. This makes a worker box able to run a session end-to-end. No config/changelog/version-bump changes.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox: src/worker (runtime, RPC clients, launch), gateway worker-environments, CLI command policy, lint-suppressions — 744 tests green, including the deep-review regression tests (stop-during-commit, resync-below-cursor renumber, live-seam-failure-does-not-abort, stale-base-leaf fail-stop, epoch-flip mid-inference, reconnect-mid-stream single provider call).
- Dedicated adversarial correctness review verified the hard parts correct (CAS/seq/replay dedupe, live ACK math, inference resume/no-double-bill, epoch fencing under withLock, restriction invariants) and found the bugs above, all fixed.
- Clean build (rm -rf dist): public plugin-SDK declaration graph 5,077,853/5,100,000; no [INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]. Type-aware lint, check:test-types, madge + import cycles zero, protocol:check, docs:map:check all green. Codex fresh autoreview clean.

target.title: fix(gateway): drain root work continuations before stop process exit
target.body:
#### What Problem This Solves

Close #105697

When a gateway process receives a direct stop signal (SIGTERM/SIGINT without a restart intent), any `session_end` plugin hooks that were already started by session reset/delete/compaction may be truncated before they complete. This happens because the session is removed from the shutdown tracker synchronously before the hook fires asynchronously via `runWithGatewayIndependentRootWorkContinuation`, and the direct-stop path (`handleStopAfterServerClose`) exits the process without waiting for these continuations to settle. Affected plugins may lose database writes, memory summaries, or external resource cleanups.

#### Why This Change Was Made

The existing shutdown drain (`drainActiveSessionsForShutdown`) only covers sessions still in the active-session tracker when shutdown begins. Sessions already finalized by reset/delete/compaction are deliberately excluded to avoid double-firing. Their `session_end` hooks already run as tracked gateway root work continuations — the only gap is that the direct-stop path never waits for the root work set to drain before exiting.

Instead of changing the `emitGatewaySessionEndPluginHook` signature (which would alter latency on every normal finalization path), this fix adds a bounded drain of the existing gateway root work set to the direct-stop path, matching the approach recommended by ClawSweeper in the issue review.

#### User Impact

No visible impact under normal operation. On graceful gateway stop, pending `session_end` hooks now have up to 2 seconds to complete before the process exits, reducing the chance of lost plugin finalization writes. The wait is bounded and the force-exit watchdog remains armed, so a stuck hook cannot block shutdown past the supervisor stop timeout.

#### Evidence

- **Type check:** `tsgo` passes with no errors
- **Tests:**
  - `gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 17 tests pass (+4: `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` success / timeout / immediate zero-count / poll-and-release)
  - `run-loop.test.ts` — 45 tests pass (+2: direct-stop drains root work before exit; warns and still exits on drain timeout; +1 mock fix)
  - `drain-active-sessions-for-shutdown.test.ts` — 28 tests pass (no regression)
- **Change scope:** 4 files, +118 lines
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.ts` — new `waitForGatewayRootWorkDrain` helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.ts` — drain call in `handleStopAfterServerClose` before `exitProcess(0)`
  - `src/process/gateway-work-admission.test.ts` — 3 new tests for drain helper
  - `src/cli/gateway-cli/run-loop.test.ts` — 2 new regression tests + mock fix
  - No config, CLI, SDK, docs, or changelog surface affected
- **No new dependencies** — reuses existing `getActiveGatewayRootWorkCount`
- **Live proof:** ran standalone script exercising `gateway-work-admission` internals under the exact race scenario:

```
=== Gateway Stop Root Work Drain — Proof Log ===

[Case 1] No pending root work — immediate return
  drain returned: true (0.1ms)
  ✓ returns true immediately
  ✓ <10ms (no busy-wait)

[Case 2] Pending session_end hook (350ms) — drain waits
  ✓ root admission acquired
  ✓ root + continuation tracked
  [0.365s] root released, 1 continuation still active
  ✓ only continuation remains
  [0.365s] SIGTERM received → starting stop drain...
  [0.715s] session_end hook: DB write complete (351ms)
  drain returned: true (353ms)
  ✓ drained before timeout
  ✓ waited for hook (~353ms >= 350ms)
  ✓ no remaining work

[Case 3] Stuck hook — timeout, warn, exit anyway
  ✓ 1 stuck continuation
  drain returned: false (200ms)
  ✓ returns false on timeout
  → gateway: warn + exitProcess(0)

[Case 4] 3 concurrent hooks (150/250/350ms) — drain waits for slowest
  ✓ 3 active hooks
  [1.071s] hook #1 done (151ms)
  [1.172s] hook #2 done (251ms)
  [1.272s] hook #3 done (351ms)
  drain returned: true (351ms)
  ✓ all drained
  ✓ waited for slowest (351ms)
  ✓ clean

=== Results: 14 passed / 0 failed ===
```

- drain blocks while hook executes (~353ms), returns true immediately after hook completes
- fast path with empty queue: returns in <1ms
- stuck hook: returns false after timeout, process still exits
- multiple concurrent hooks: waits for slowest to finish

target.title: fix(cli): restore terminal state before exit in logs and hooks commands
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`process.exit(1)` in `logs-cli.ts:685` and `hooks-cli.ts:153` bypasses the CLI's standard exit path (`runtime.exit()`), which calls `restoreTerminalState()` before terminating. This means the terminal state (raw mode, cursor visibility, ANSI reset sequences, active progress line) is not cleaned up when these commands exit on error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Every other CLI command uses `runtime.exit()` → `restoreTerminalState()` → `process.exit()` as defined in `src/runtime.ts:89-96`. These two call sites were the only exceptions. A review of the commit history shows no evidence this was intentional — the `process.exit(1)` was introduced during the initial monorepo import and never revisited.

## User Impact

Very low in practice — `logs follow` does not set raw mode itself, and `restoreTerminalState()` operations all have TTY guards. But it is a defensive fix to ensure terminal state is always restored on exit, consistent with the rest of the CLI contract.

## Evidence

- **Contract**: `src/runtime.ts:89-96` — `defaultRuntime.exit()` calls `restoreTerminalState("runtime exit", ...)` before `process.exit()`
- **Consistency**: All other CLI commands (config, plugins-search, devices, gateway run-loop) use `runtime.exit()`
- **Commit history**: `git blame` confirms the raw `process.exit(1)` was added in the initial monorepo import commit with no subsequent discussion or adjustment
- **Tests**: `logs-cli.test.ts` (5/5), `hooks-cli.test.ts` (37/37) — all passing

## Changes

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/cli/logs-cli.ts` | Import `restoreTerminalState` and call it before `process.exit(1)` on unrecoverable follow error |
| `src/cli/hooks-cli.ts` | Replace `process.exit(1)` with `defaultRuntime.exit(1)` (already imported) |

target.title: fix(cron): filter non-string env entries instead of silently deleting the entire env block
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #105433.

When a cron schedule config contains a non-string environment variable (e.g. `env: { DEBUG: true }`), the normalization function `normalizeTrimmedStringRecord` encounters the non-string value and returns `undefined`. The caller at `normalize.ts:286-293` then executes `delete next.env` — **silently discarding the entire env block**, including any valid entries alongside the invalid one.

For example, with `env: { DEBUG: true, API_KEY: "secret", PATH: "/usr/bin" }`:
- **Before**: All three entries are lost — `API_KEY` and `PATH` silently deleted
- **After**: `API_KEY` and `PATH` are preserved, only `DEBUG` is filtered out

## Root Cause

`normalizeTrimmedStringRecord` (`src/cron/normalize.ts:57-71`) uses an all-or-nothing bail-out: when any entry has a non-string value, `return undefined` discards the entire record. This is unnecessarily destructive — env entries are independent, and one bad entry should not invalidate the rest.

## Fix

Change the invalid-entry handling from bail-out to skip:

```diff
-    if (!key || val === undefined) {
-      return undefined;
-    }
+    if (!key || val === undefined) {
+      continue;
     }
+  if (entries.length === 0) {
+    return undefined;
+  }
```

Two behavioural properties preserved:
- When **all** entries are invalid → return `undefined` (trigger deletion)
- When **some** entries are valid → return only the valid ones

A secondary bug is also fixed: a blank/whitespace-only key previously caused the entire block to be discarded; it is now correctly skipped.

## Files Changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/cron/normalize.ts` | Two lines changed in `normalizeTrimmedStringRecord` |
| `src/cron/normalize.test.ts` | 3 new regression tests |

## Testing / Proof

```
node -e verification script:
Test 1: Mixed valid/invalid env
  Input: {"DEBUG":true,"FOO":"bar","COUNT":42,"PATH":"/usr/bin"}
  Old:   undefined <- BUG: entire block deleted!
  New:   {"FOO":"bar","PATH":"/usr/bin"} <- FIX: only valid entries kept
  PASS:  YES

Test 2: All non-string values
  Old: undefined (correct: undefined = delete)
  New: undefined (correct: undefined = delete)

Test 3: All valid string values
  Old: {"FOO":"bar","PATH":"/usr/bin"} (correct: preserved)
  New: {"FOO":"bar","PATH":"/usr/bin"} (correct: preserved)

Test 4: Empty key trimming
  Old: undefined  (empty key → lost everything!)
  New: {"FOO":"bar"} (empty key correctly skipped)

Test 5: Non-object input
  Old: undefined (unchanged)
  New: undefined (unchanged)
```

### New regression tests in `normalize.test.ts`:

| Test | Scenario |
|------|----------|
| filters non-string env values instead of silently deleting the entire env block | `{ DEBUG: true, FOO: "bar", COUNT: 42, PATH: "/usr/bin" }` → `{ FOO: "bar", PATH: "/usr/bin" }` |
| deletes the entire env block when every entry is non-string | `{ DEBUG: true, COUNT: 42 }` → `env` key removed |
| preserves env when it contains only valid string values | `{ FOO: "bar", PATH: "/usr/bin" }` → preserved unchanged (no regression) |

target.title: fix(sessions): cap in-memory session history to prevent unbounded growth
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Long-running autonomous sessions accumulate message turns indefinitely in `SessionHistorySseState.sentHistory.messages` without any pruning. The in-memory array grows without bound, leading to OOM crashes on constrained hosts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two improvements:

**1. Early raw-message trimming (new):** The constructor now trims the initial raw messages to `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES × 2` (1000) BEFORE the full `projectChatDisplayMessages` pass when inline mode is active. This avoids projecting and transforming thousands of raw messages only to discard most of them immediately.

**2. Projected-message capping:** `appendInlineMessage` caps `sentHistory.messages` at `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES` (500) after every append via `trimHistoryMessages`. Combined with early raw trimming, this ensures both the raw-input and projected-output paths are bounded.

When trimming, `hasMore` is set to `true` and `nextCursor` points to the first retained seq so callers can signal older-history availability. The cap only applies to inline (unpaginated) mode.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes during long-running autonomous sessions
- Older history remains available via `refreshAsync()` or paginated snapshots
- Normal interactive sessions (≤500 turns) are completely unaffected
- Inline SSE appends continue to work for recent history

## Persistent Data Model — No migration needed

The change does not modify any serialized data format, SQLite schema, config surface, or storage layout. The `sentHistory` array is strictly in-memory state reconstructed from transcript reads on each session load.

## Evidence

### A. Unit tests — 96 passing

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/session-history-state.test.ts

 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  96 passed (96)
```

### B. Before/after comparison


## What Problem This Solves

Closes #105803

When a provider config sets `contextWindow` and `maxTokens` at the provider
level (documented as defaults for models under that provider), `applyModelDefaults`
in `src/config/defaults.ts` ignored them. Models that omitted these fields
silently received `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_TOKENS` / `DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_TOKENS` instead.

Provider-level `contextTokens` inheritance is addressed separately in #105841.

## Evidence

**Before** — model without contextWindow/maxTokens gets global defaults:
```
model.contextWindow === 200000 (DEFAULT_CONTEXT_TOKENS)
model.maxTokens === 8192 (DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_TOKENS)
```

**After** — model inherits provider-level defaults:
```
model.contextWindow === 50000 (from provider config)
model.maxTokens === 4096 (from provider config)
```

**Tests** (3 new + 18 existing = 21 pass):
```
 ✓ inherits provider-level contextWindow when model omits it
 ✓ lets per-model contextWindow override provider-level default
 ✓ clamps provider-level maxTokens to the resolved contextWindow
```

## Why This Change Was Made

`ModelProviderConfig` exposes `contextWindow` and `maxTokens` as provider-level
defaults, documented in `docs/concepts/model-providers.md`. The runtime path
(#44786) already respects provider-level defaults for discovered models, but
the static config-loading path (`applyModelDefaults`) only looked at per-model
values.

## Merge Risk

Low — 7-line change in a well-tested function. Per-model overrides still
take precedence; the fallback chain is now model → provider → global default,
matching the documented behavior.

target.title: fix(config): propagate provider-level contextTokens default to models (#105821)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`models.providers.*.contextTokens` is documented as a provider-level default effective runtime context cap for models under that provider. However, `applyModelDefaults` in `src/config/defaults.ts` only considered per-model `contextTokens`, so models that omitted the field did not inherit the provider default.

## Why This Change Was Made

The runtime already falls back to provider-level `contextTokens` in `applyConfiguredContextWindows`, but config consumers that read the materialized model entries—such as `openclaw models list` and config snapshots—saw `undefined` and omitted the effective cap. This brings `applyModelDefaults` in line with the documented contract and with the existing provider-level `api` default propagation.

## User Impact

Users who set `contextTokens` on a provider will now see the inherited cap reflected for every model under that provider in `openclaw models list` and other config-aware surfaces, unless a model explicitly overrides it.

## Evidence

### Unit tests
Added regression tests in `src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts`:

- `propagates provider-level contextTokens default to models` fails before the fix (`contextTokens` is `undefined`) and passes after (`120000`).
- `lets per-model contextTokens override provider-level default` confirms explicit model values still win.

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/model-alias-defaults.test.ts --run
# Test Files  1 passed (1)
# Tests  20 passed (20)
```

### Real CLI output
Config (`~/.openclaw/openclaw.json`, redacted):

```json
{
  "models": {
    "providers": {
      "demo-provider": {
        "baseUrl": "https://demo-provider.example.test/v1",
        "apiKey": "sk-demo-redacted",
        "api": "openai-completions",
        "contextTokens": 120000,
        "models": [
          { "id": "inherited-cap", "name": "Inherited cap model", "contextWindow": 200000, "maxTokens": 8192 },
          { "id": "overridden-cap", "name": "Overridden cap model", "contextWindow": 200000, "maxTokens": 8192, "contextTokens": 96000 }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

After the fix, `openclaw models list --json --no-color` shows the inherited cap on the first model and the explicit override on the second:

```json
{
  "count": 2,
  "models": [
    {
      "key": "demo-provider/inherited-cap",
      "name": "Inherited cap model",
      "input": "text",
      "contextWindow": 200000,
      "contextTokens": 120000,
      "local": false,
      "available": true,
      "tags": ["default"],
      "missing": false
    },
    {
      "key": "demo-provider/overridden-cap",
      "name": "Overridden cap model",
      "input": "text",
      "contextWindow": 200000,
      "contextTokens": 96000,
      "local": false,
      "available": true,
      "tags": [],
      "missing": false
    }
  ]
}
```

Before the fix, the first row omitted `contextTokens` entirely.

Fixes #105821

target.title: fix(config): warn when JSON5 comments are lost on config write
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw uses JSON5 to parse user configurations (supporting comments), but writes them back with JSON.stringify which silently strips all user-authored comments on every automatic config write.

## Why This Change Was Made

JSON5.parse discards comments during parsing — they cannot survive the parse-modify-stringify roundtrip without an AST-aware library. The fix adds a string-aware `hasJSON5Comments()` detector that strips string literals before checking for comment markers, then warns users when their comments will be lost.

## User Impact

- Users with JSON5 comments in config now see a warning before their comments are stripped
- URLs inside strings (`http://...`) do not cause false warnings
- Inline `//` comments (`{a:1 // note}`) are correctly detected
- JSON5 line continuations (backslash+newline in strings) do not cause false warnings
- Plain JSON configs produce no warning

## Evidence

```
$ node -e

✅ detect  "// comment"                       → true   line-start comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 // inline
}"                  → true   inline // comment
✅ detect  "/* block */"                      → true   block comment
✅ detect  "{a:1 /* inline */}"               → true   inline block comment
✅ ignore  "\"http://url\""                   → false  URL in string
✅ ignore  "\"// not comment\""               → false  // in string
✅ ignore  "\"foo\\\n// still string\""       → false  line-continued // in string
✅ ignore  "{\"a\":1}"                       → false  plain JSON

11/11 passed
```

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/schema.test.ts

```

```
$ npx oxfmt --check src/config/io.ts
```

target.title: fix(ios): block omitted share attachments
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #103363.

The iOS Share Extension accepted at most three image attachments and ignored videos, files, PDFs, and unknown attachment providers while still moving toward the normal send flow. That let a user share partial content without any visible explanation.

## Why This Change Was Made

This keeps the current gateway media contract unchanged: the share route still sends image attachments only, and it does not attempt to add video/PDF/file transport in this PR.

Instead, extraction now records selected image count, accepted image count, and unsupported attachment classes. If the extension would omit selected content, the compose card enters the existing blocked state with a concrete recovery message, so send stays disabled until the user removes omitted items and shares again.

## User Impact

- Sharing 6 images now shows: `Only 3 of 6 images can be sent. Remove omitted items and share again.`
- Sharing a video, PDF/file, or unknown attachment now shows an unsupported-item message instead of silently sending only text or the first accepted images.
- Normal shares with up to 3 images are unchanged.

## Evidence

Focused local proof:

```text
SHARE_ATTACHMENT_SUMMARY_PROOF=PASS
Only 3 of 6 images can be sent. Remove omitted items and share again.
OpenClaw Share cannot send 1 video(s), 2 file(s), 1 unsupported item(s) yet. Remove omitted items and share again.
```

Validation run:

```text
swiftc /tmp/.../ShareAttachmentSummary.swift /tmp/.../main.swift -o /tmp/.../share-proof && /tmp/.../share-proof
git diff HEAD^ HEAD --check
```

### Real proof

Exact-head native simulator proof for `5dda9040ac66350805428609bca660dd5373e6f6`.

Environment: iPhone 17 Pro simulator, iOS 26.2 (`23C54`), Xcode 27.0. The installed app's `OpenClawGitCommit` is the exact PR head above. Both scenarios used the real Photos → Share Sheet → OpenClaw Share Extension path.

#### Six-image omission path

- Selected 6 photos in Photos.
- The extension rendered: `Only 3 of 6 images can be sent. Remove omitted items and share again.`
- Send was disabled.
- After entering `Compare all six images`, Send remained disabled.
- XCTest result: **Passed** (`39.91s`).

![Six selected images show the omission warning with Send disabled](https://files.catbox.moe/91crio.png)

#### Normal one-image control

- Selected 1 photo in Photos.
- After entering `Describe this image`, Send enabled normally.
- XCTest result: **Passed** (`27.65s`).

![A normal one-image share enables Send after draft text is entered](https://files.catbox.moe/1vcxn8.png)

Focused commands:

```text

xcodebuild ... -only-testing:OpenClawUITests/ShareExtensionUITests/testOneSelectedImageStillEnablesSendAfterDraftText test
```

The UI-test additions were a local proof harness only; no test or product files were pushed to the contributor branch.

target.title: fix(sessions): cap in-memory session history to prevent unbounded growth
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Long-running autonomous sessions accumulate message turns indefinitely in `SessionHistorySseState.sentHistory.messages` without any pruning. The in-memory array grows without bound, leading to OOM crashes on constrained hosts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two improvements:

**1. Early raw-message trimming (new):** The constructor now trims the initial raw messages to `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES × 2` (1000) BEFORE the full `projectChatDisplayMessages` pass when inline mode is active. This avoids projecting and transforming thousands of raw messages only to discard most of them immediately.

**2. Projected-message capping:** `appendInlineMessage` caps `sentHistory.messages` at `MAX_INLINE_HISTORY_MESSAGES` (500) after every append via `trimHistoryMessages`. Combined with early raw trimming, this ensures both the raw-input and projected-output paths are bounded.

When trimming, `hasMore` is set to `true` and `nextCursor` points to the first retained seq so callers can signal older-history availability. The cap only applies to inline (unpaginated) mode.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM crashes during long-running autonomous sessions
- Older history remains available via `refreshAsync()` or paginated snapshots
- Normal interactive sessions (≤500 turns) are completely unaffected
- Inline SSE appends continue to work for recent history

## Persistent Data Model — No migration needed

The change does not modify any serialized data format, SQLite schema, config surface, or storage layout. The `sentHistory` array is strictly in-memory state reconstructed from transcript reads on each session load.

## Evidence

### A. Unit tests — 96 passing

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/session-history-state.test.ts

 Test Files  4 passed (4)
      Tests  96 passed (96)
```

### B. Before/after comparison

```
     100 turns  |  before:   100  after:  100  saved:     0 (0.0%)  ✅
     500 turns  |  before:   500  after:  500  saved:     0 (0.0%)  ✅
    1000 turns  |  before:  1000  after:  500  saved:   500 (50.0%)  ✅
    5000 turns  |  before:  5000  after:  500  saved:  4500 (90.0%)  ✅
   10000 turns  |  before: 10000  after:  500  saved:  9500 (95.0%)  ✅
```

### C. Cursor pagination — 2500 messages fully retrievable

```

  Page 5:  500 msgs [1→500]      cursor=-     hasMore=false

```

### D. Lint + type check

```

```

target.title: fix: inherit provider-level contextWindow/maxTokens when applying model defaults
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Closes #105803

When a provider config sets `contextWindow` and `maxTokens` at the provider
level (documented as defaults for models under that provider), `applyModelDefaults`
in `src/config/defaults.ts` ignored them. Models that omitted these fields
silently received `DEFAULT_CONTEXT_TOKENS` / `DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_TOKENS` instead.

Provider-level `contextTokens` inheritance is addressed separately in #105841.

## Evidence

**Before** — model without contextWindow/maxTokens gets global defaults:
```
model.contextWindow === 200000 (DEFAULT_CONTEXT_TOKENS)
model.maxTokens === 8192 (DEFAULT_MODEL_MAX_TOKENS)
```

**After** — model inherits provider-level defaults:
```
model.contextWindow === 50000 (from provider config)
model.maxTokens === 4096 (from provider config)
```

**Tests** (3 new + 18 existing = 21 pass):
```
 ✓ inherits provider-level contextWindow when model omits it
 ✓ lets per-model contextWindow override provider-level default
 ✓ clamps provider-level maxTokens to the resolved contextWindow
```

## Why This Change Was Made

`ModelProviderConfig` exposes `contextWindow` and `maxTokens` as provider-level
defaults, documented in `docs/concepts/model-providers.md`. The runtime path
(#44786) already respects provider-level defaults for discovered models, but
the static config-loading path (`applyModelDefaults`) only looked at per-model
values.

## Merge Risk

Low — 7-line change in a well-tested function. Per-model overrides still
take precedence; the fallback chain is now model → provider → global default,
matching the documented behavior.
